title: Auto-Reclosing Promotion via Optimized Secondary Arc Harmonics Suppression in Hybrid AC/DC Systems
abstract: The integration of hybrid AC/DC transmission lines introduces significant challenges in power system protection. Harmonic-rich secondary arc currents (SAC) prolong extinction time, leading to relay malfunctions and auto-reclosing failures. This study proposes a genetic optimization framework for secondary arc harmonics (SAH) mitigation, employing an online design technique through synchronized PSCAD-MATLAB simulations based on the Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). Optimized passive filters are designed for both baseline (AC/AC) and hybrid configurations. Results demonstrate that hybrid systems achieve superior SAH suppression with reduced filter requirements, highlighting their economic advantage over conventional lines. Experimental protection relay tests validate the proposed approach, confirming its effectiveness in enhancing system protection.

title: Quasi-Model Prediction Based Fault-Tolerant Control With No Redundancy for Modular Multilevel Converters
abstract: The fault-tolerant control is the crucial technology to guarantee the reliability and continuity of operation for modular multilevel converter (MMC). However, the fault-tolerant efficacy of MMC is limited by the number of redundant submodules (SMs). This paper proposes a fault-tolerant control with no redundancy to enhance the reliability of MMC. In this control, the DC voltage adjustment and the phase angle shift are united to exert functions. Based on the mechanisms of the two measures, the quasi-model prediction scheme including: the detailed model, cost function and optimization seeking method is established to provide the optimal parameters for the fault tolerance. With this scheme, the proposed fault-tolerant control effectively improves the shortcomings of the existing methods. Multiple perspective comparisons show that this proposed control has the advantages of better output performance, stronger fault tackling capability and lighter computation burden. The reliable and high-quality operation of MMC can be well kept after redundant SMs are completely exhausted. The feasibility of the fault-tolerant control is validated by the simulation results in Matlab/Simulink.

title: Influence of Pipeline Vibration on Heavy Gas Action Characteristics of Gas Relay in Oil-immersed Transformer
abstract: Gas relays serve as vital non-electrical protective elements for transformers but occasionally experience maloperations in their heavy gas action during actual operation. To investigate the underlying causes, this study explores the response of heavy-gas protection in BF-type double-float gas relays to pipeline vibration. The constructed experimental platform, coupled with a fluid-solid coupling dynamic model, characterises heavy gas action behaviors under transient oil flow and pipeline vibration excitations. Simulation and experimental results show a downward trend in the heavy gas action flow velocity of the BF-type double-float gas relay with increasing pipeline vibration. Specifically, numerical findings reveal that pipeline vibrations of 32–40 g reduce the heavy gas setting flow velocity by 12.34%–14.29%. Meanwhile, fluid-solid coupling simulations confirm that vibration enhances the turbulence intensity of the flow field and unsteady pressure fluctuations, which disrupt the force balance by superimposing vibration torque, leading to premature triggering of the action. The proposed vibration-oil flow coupling model reveals how pipeline vibration triggers relay maloperation. These findings provide a theoretical basis for optimizing setting values and developing anti-maloperation strategies.

title: Line Equivalent Based Short-Circuit Current Calculation in Distribution Networks with Numerous Inverter Interfaced Distributed Generators
abstract: The calculation of short-circuit current (SCC) is crucial for planning, operation and maintenance of distribution systems. The integration of Inverter-Interfaced Distributed Generators (IIDGs) into distribution systems induces nonlinear characteristics, which make the traditional nodal voltage equation-based SCC calculation methods ineffective. To balance the SCC calculation accuracy and efficiency, a line equivalent based SCC calculation method is proposed to address the increasing integration of IIDGs in distribution networks. Firstly, an aggregation zoning method for IIDGs is proposed based on their fault response characteristics. Both the Low Voltage Ride Through (LVRT) controlling and fault steady-state voltage drop are considered. Then, an equivalent model of the non-fault line, utilizing piecewise equivalence, is established to simplify the network structure. Finally, the post-fault node voltages and branch currents are determined by solving the nodal voltage equation of the established simplified network with fixed-point iteration. Simulation results demonstrate the proposed algorithm has satisfactory accuracy and computation time in calculating SCC of distribution networks with numerous IIDGs.

title: Optimization of Transient Overvoltage Suppression At the Multi-Outfeed HVDC System Considering Cascading Commutation Failure
abstract: In a multi-outfeed HVDC system, rectifier stations are closely spaced and tightly coupled, which facilitates the propagation of disturbances to adjacent HVDC links. When a commutation failure (CF) happens in a faulted HVDC system, the resulting transient overvoltage (TOV) at the sending end (SE) can cause a voltage rise in an adjacent unfaulted HVDC system, potentially triggering cascading CF and thereby expanding the fault impact. To mitigate these risks, a refined optimization method is developed in this study for the regulation of rectifier-side TOV, specifically incorporating the immunity constraints of adjacent links against cascading CF. First, the impact and evolution process of how TOV at the SE of a faulted HVDC system leads to cascading CF in adjacent unfaulted HVDC links are analyzed, and the mathematical boundary for rectifier-side bus potential is established, which serves to prevent CF in unfaulted HVDC system. Accordingly, an optimized DC current regulation scheme is proposed, aiming to constrain transient voltage rises while ensuring the commutation security of adjacent HVDC links. Finally, simulation studies based on a multi-outfeed HVDC system model in PSCAD/EMTDC are carried out to demonstrate the performance of the proposed method.

title: Reliability Assessment of Distribution Systems With Microgrids Using Discrete-Time Markov Chains
abstract: Microgrids can improve the reliability and resiliency of modern distribution systems. The stochasticity of local non-dispatchable distributed energy resources (NDDERs), combined with the time-dependency of battery energy storage systems (BESSs) and load shedding strategies (LSSs), complicates the reliability assessment of distribution networks embedded with microgrids. In this work, we propose a minimal cut-set method using a discrete-time Markov chain to perform the time-series adequacy assessment. Our method offers an alternative to sequential Monte Carlo simulations (SMCSs) to account for the stochasticity of NDDERs and the time-dependency of BESSs and LSSs. Case studies on modified IEEE-RTBS Bus2 and IEEE 123-Test Feeder systems assess the accuracy of the method when compared with SMCSs.

title: A Uniform Grid-Forming Control of Multi-Terminal DC Systems
abstract: The control of a multi-terminal dc (MTDC) system is challenging due to the flexible control modes of ac-dc converter stations at different terminals. In this paper, a uniform grid forming control method is proposed, which can be applied to all ac-dc converter stations at all terminals of a MTDC system. It can provide the grid-forming and damping effects, and meanwhile achieve the transfer of these effects among the whole system. The different extension formats of the proposed control method are analyzed. The steady-state power flow and the small signal stability of the whole MTDC system are comprehensively discussed. The time-domain simulations of a five-terminal dc system with renewable energy generation and energy storage are conducted, to validate the corresponding theoretical analysis.

title: Discrimination of Tree-Contact High-Impedance and Flame Faults in Distribution Networks via Zero-Sequence Voltage Monitoring
abstract: Tree-contact high-impedance faults (THIF) and flame faults are common fault types in the forest area. Their mitigation and prevention are crucial to the management of distribution network faults. However, the signals of these faults are so weak that existing zero-sequence protection methods cannot ensure effectiveness and accuracy during the early fault stage. To address this issue, this paper investigates the electro-thermal coupling mechanism during the fault evolution process. Fault resistance models are established for different fault types. Experiments on 10 kV and 35 kV distribution systems verify that the proposed models can effectively capture the time-varying characteristics of the faults. Then electrical characteristics are investigated during discharges by applying Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to the zero-sequence voltage. Feature parameters are obtained including Total Harmonic Distortion (THD), Power Spectral Entropy (PSE), Skewness (SKE) and Kurtosis (KUR) of the sub-fundamental spectral components. Statistical analysis is employed to mitigate the influence of individual sample variability. From the experimental results, the frequency domain characteristics of both THIF and flame faults are independent of voltage levels. THD of flame fault is significantly higher than that of THIF due to the unstable discharge path in the flame. Conversely, THIF shows higher SKE and KUR because of low-frequency turbulence in the flame. The combined unstable discharge channel and turbulence cause PSE to be significantly higher in flame fault than in THIF. This research provides a methodological basis for fault classification and prevention for both 10 kV and 35 kV distribution lines.

title: Resilient Cable Rating for Overplanted Wind Farms Tackling Data Imbalance and Aging Risks
abstract: Increasing wind farm capacity via overplanting enhances energy production but risks accelerating cable aging if transmission capacity is poorly managed. Consequently, resilient Dynamic Cable Rating (DCR) prediction-defined as the ability to maintain stability under data quality degradation and operational shifts-is crucial for reliable operation. However, achieving this is challenged by limited datasets, missing data, and complex spatio-temporal correlations. To address these issues, a resilient DCR prediction and thermal estimation framework is developed. First, a Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (CGAN) is applied to synthetically augment limited datasets, effectively resolving the load data imbalance. Second, a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Residual Shrinkage Network (STGARSN) is proposed. This model integrates an extended Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network with Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) and a graph attention mechanism to capture complex correlations. Crucially, it incorporates a residual shrinkage module to filter noise and outliers, thereby ensuring model resilience. Finally, to optimize economic performance while minimizing cable aging, a comparative analysis of various overplanting strategies is conducted. Experiments on real cable temperature measurements demonstrate the superior resilience of the proposed model, maintaining high accuracy not only across different forecasting horizons but also under conditions of missing data and sensor noise. The proposed framework accurately predicts DCR and supports long-term offshore wind farm operations through improved economic and technical decision-making.

title: Distribution System Overhead Switch Bare Copper Contact Degradation: Copper Oxide Impedance, Thickness, and Composition
abstract: Overhead (OH) medium-voltage air-break electric distribution switches with bare copper contacts located within a six-mile proximity of the Pacific Ocean coast in San Diego Gas & Electric's (SDG&E) service territory have been observed with corrosion and have a higher replacement rate than similarly aged OH inland switches which do not exhibit the same corrosion growth. These OH failures are associated with extended outages, increased System Average Interruption Duration Index (SAIDI), and increased System Average Interruption Frequency Index (SAIFI). This research has been investigating copper corrosion properties leading to the formation of high-impedance oxides that may be associated with OH bare copper contact switch failure along the coast. Using scanningelectron microscopy (SEM), and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) the copper oxide thickness, impedance, and composition were quantified. Cuprite and atacamite were identified as the two primary copper oxides formed at the surface of the switches. Atacamite was the thickest oxide layer identified. Cuprite and atacamite were found to have significantly higher impedance than bare copper. The oxides’ impedance could restrict current flow, leading to increased contact heating. As a conclusion, bare copper contact switches should not be installed in areas near the coast.

title: Systematic Predictive Modeling of Moisture Dynamics for Condition Assessment of Paper-Liquid Insulation System of Transformer
abstract: In this study, we present a computationally efficient model for predicting moisture dynamics in paper-liquid insulation systems of transformers, aimed at enhancing real-time condition assessment and operational reliability. Moisture migration between cellulose insulation and dielectric liquids (mineral oil, natural ester, synthetic ester) is governed by temperature-dependent diffusion processes, which significantly influence insulation aging and dielectric performance. The proposed model applies Fick's second law with a diffusion coefficient dependent on moisture content, temperature, and insulation thickness. The governing equations are solved using an implicit finite difference scheme combined with the Tridiagonal Matrix Algorithm (TDMA), ensuring numerical stability and computational speed. Moisture equilibrium at the cellulose-liquid interface is modeled thermodynamically, assuming a constant total water content and instantaneous equilibrium. Three dynamic loading scenarios-a heat run test, IEEE C57.91-2011 Annex G, and IEC 60076-7 profiles-demonstrate the model's accuracy and adaptability. Results show that synthetic ester exhibits superior moisture absorption, leading to enhanced drying of cellulose insulation. Due to its simplicity and computational efficiency, the model is well-suited for integration into online monitoring systems and digital twin frameworks for transformer asset management.

title: Dynamic Thermal Network Model Based Temperature Rise Characteristics Analysis for OPGW Ice-Melting Process
abstract: The icing of optical fiber composite overhead ground wires (OPGW) poses a serious threat to power supply reliability, necessitating timely de-icing operations using the short-circuit current ice-melting method. However, excessive ice-melting currents may cause the optical fiber temperature to exceed design thresholds, thereby jeopardizing grid safety. To enable the appropriate selection of ice-melting currents, we first develop a dynamic thermal network model (TNM) that considers both radial and tangential heat transfer, incorporating variations in thermal parameters resulting from the melting of the ice layer. Subsequently, the proposed dynamic TNM is validated using the finite element method. Then, based on the established dynamic TNM, the temperature rise characteristics and influencing factors during the OPGW ice-melting processes are investigated. Finally, from the perspective of the whole-process temperature rise characteristics of the outer surface of OPGW and the optical fiber, this paper proposes the method for selecting the minimum and maximum ice-melting currents. The proposed method ensures that the optical fiber remains within a safe temperature range throughout the ice-melting process, contributing significantly to the safe operation of the power grid.

title: Faulty Feeder Detection Under High Impedance Faults Based on Harmonics of Calculated Fault Currents in Resonant Grounding Network
abstract: The identification of faulty feeders under high impedance faults (HIF) presents significant challenges due to weak fault currents and the difficulty in capturing transient components. Instead of relying on transient features, this paper proposes a faulty-feeder detection method for HIFs based on the harmonic characteristics of the calculated fault currents, and it is effective throughout the HIFs duration, which are immune from the fault triggering time. Firstly, the fault characteristics under HIFs are analyzed considering the nonlinear arcs, revealing that harmonic currents predominantly presented in the faulty feeder can be utilized for identification. Secondly, the fault currents at the fault points are calculated by subtracting the capacitive currents from the faulty-feeder zero-sequence currents (ZSC), significantly enhancing the nonlinear features in the ZSCs, whereas the calculated currents for healthy feeders essentially remain as capacitive currents with few arc-related distortions. A two-step fundamental component shift method is then developed to extract harmonic currents from these calculated fault currents. Thirdly, the energy proportion and kurtosis value are applied to describe the fault features of the extracted harmonics. Finally, a comprehensive detection scheme integrating harmonic energy and kurtosis criterion is proposed. Various test verifications demonstrate the feasibility and reliability of the proposed method.

title: Sequential Switching Modeling and Transient Instability Mechanism for MMC-HVDC Receiving-End Systems with Fault Ride-Through
abstract: Previous literature shows that the second-order phase-locked loop dynamics dominate the transient stability of high voltage direct current system based on modular multilevel converter (MMC-HVDC) in the during-fault stage. The effects of DC-link dynamics and transient behavior after fault recovery have rarely been studied. Focusing on the post-fault stage, this paper first develops a transient model in each fault stage based on the typical fault ride-through strategy, considering the DC-link voltage dynamics. Although the during-fault stage is stable, the MMC-HVDC system still faces the risk of transient instability in the post-fault stage under receiving-end AC weak grid faults because of DC voltage deviation. The angular frequency jumps that occur in both the during-fault stage and post-fault stage are uncovered. High-dimensional basin-of-attraction analysis reveals that the angular frequency jump generated by the DC-link voltage dynamics can weaken the resynchronization capability. Moreover, based on the proposed transient stability margin index, the parameter feasible region under different ramp coefficients, DC voltage droop coefficients, and short circuit ratios is obtained. Finally, hardware-in-the-loop experiments are conducted to validate the results of the theoretical analysis.

title: Assessing emission limits in the supraharmonic 20 to150 kHz range
abstract: Measurements of the frequency-dependent network impedance in the frequency range 20-150 kHz have been carried out on points of common coupling in residential areas, office buildings, street cabinets, transformers, individual residence metering cabinets, and the Per Högström laboratory in Luleå University, located in the North of Sweden. The results of the measurements are presented. A method for representing the network impedance in the form of a finite number of lumped R-L C elements is proposed in this paper, based on measurements. Based on the measurements and lumped parameters, the emission limits in the frequency range 20-150 kHz have been identified and presented in this paper. In the absence of measurements, a method for identifying emission limits based on the extended IEC 61000 4-7 reference impedance using Monte Carlo analysis has been presented. As EV charging assumes prevalence in terms of loads on the grid, a comparative analysis of the change in grid impedance with the introduction of EVs on the grid is presented.

title: Apparent Impedances and Distribution of Fault Currents for Solid Faults in 2x25kV Electric Railway Systems
abstract: This article analyzes the distribution of short-circuit currents in 2x25kV electric railway systems, as well as the apparent impedances seen by the distance protection for solid faults. The analyzed short-circuit types are catenary-to-ground, feeder-to-ground and catenary-to-feeder. The line model is based on a 2x2 matrix in cases with only one track, and on 3x3 and 4x4 matrices in cases with two tracks. Simplified analytical models are deduced, neglecting transformer impedances and train currents in order to explain more clearly the distribution of currents under short-circuit conditions, as well as the parabolic behavior of the modulus of apparent impedances as a function of the distance up to the fault. The effect of transformer impedances is shown with the help of the numerical solution of the network.

title: Fatigue Fragility Curves for Overhead Conductors Subjected to Varying Amplitude at Suspension Clamps
abstract: Overhead conductors undergo multiple cycles of varying bending amplitude at suspension clamps due to aeolian vibration. The current approach for evaluating fretting fatigue damage relies on using constant amplitude experimental tests on conductor classes grouped according to the Poffenberger-Swart relation. This approach neglects the effect of sequence of amplitudes. A probabilistic fatigue life assessment model is developed using the Poisson binomial model and various cumulative damage theories for sets of vibrations with different amplitudes. Fragility curves are presented for the failure of the first wire to the fourth wire failure in a conductor for experimental data sets with increasing and decreasing amplitudes of vibration. A comparison of predicted fragility curves with the conductor fatigue data shows that although the contact stresses as a function of amplitude of vibration are independent of the loading sequence, the material fatigue resistance is affected by the loading sequence. Cumulative damage theories that include the order of loading on the wires predict fragilities that are closer to experimental observations.

title: Transient Voltage Stability Analysis and Enhancement of Grid-Following Converters Considering DC-link Voltage Control Dynamics
abstract: With the large-scale integration of renewable energy resources through grid-following converters, the voltage support capability of the system is weakened, thereby increasing the risk of voltage instability. Existing studies mainly focus on the transient voltage stability of induction motors (IMs), where the dynamics of voltage source converters (VSCs) are often neglected. However, VSCs with DC-link voltage control (DVC) also face the risk of transient voltage instability under grid faults, even when the voltage-supporting effect of VSCs during low-voltage ride through (LVRT) is considered. Such an instability phenomenon poses a tremendous threat to the stable operation of VSC-dominated power systems, which has not been addressed in existing research. To fill this gap, this paper provides a theoretical explanation of the VSC's transient performance under DVC and LVRT, and reveals the transient voltage instability mechanism of modern power systems with high penetration of VSCs. To mitigate such instability, this paper proposes an adaptive current-limiting control strategy after analyzing the impact of current limitation on transient voltage stability. Simulation results verify the correctness of the theoretical analysis and the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy.

title: Spring Operating Mechanism Condition Monitoring Based on MEMS Pressure Sensors
abstract: With the advancement of smart grids, the reliable monitoring of operating mechanisms in GIS circuit breakers has become a key factor in ensuring the safe operation of power systems. This study proposes a condition monitoring method for spring operating mechanisms based on MEMS pressure sensors. A miniaturized MEMS sensor is innovatively embedded inside the breaker's operating mechanism to directly measure the closing spring force, enabling precise monitoring of the energy storage, closing, and opening processes. Compared with conventional indirect methods relying on coil current or motor current signals, the proposed approach provides more direct mechanical information and, through multi-signal collaborative analysis, allows for more accurate identification of key operating stages and state transitions. The method is systematically validated by theoretical modeling, ANSYS simulation, laboratory experiments, and field tests. The results demonstrate that the MEMS pressure sensor significantly improves monitoring accuracy and stability, while its miniaturized and non-intrusive design ensures negligible impact on the mechanism's structure and normal operation. Furthermore, experimental measurements show strong consistency with theoretical calculations and simulation results, confirming the engineering feasibility of the method. This work not only enhances the accuracy of operating mechanism condition identification but also provides new technical support for intelligent maintenance and fault prediction of GIS circuit breakers, offering important practical value.

title: Functional Requirements for Ultrafast Thomson Coil Actuator in Arc Commutation Hybrid DC Circuit Breaker
abstract: Hybrid DC circuit breakers featuring an ultrafast Thomson coil actuator are a key technology for enabling envisioned medium voltage DC grids. Particularly, the design of the actuator is considered challenging and has therefore been addressed in research for more than 20 years. These investigations have focused on actuators in conjunction with current injection type DC circuit breakers. However, these results cannot be transferred to arc commutation hybrid DC circuit breakers. For this breaker topology, the interaction between actuator parameters and breaker performance is not well understood, yet it is essential in order to define functional requirements for the actuator. This paper provides the first investigation of this interaction, by integrating an analysis of the commutation process into the design consideration. New insights regarding the contact separation time of the actuator and its implications to the overall circuit breaker performance are presented. Resulting feasible operating regions of the actuator are established—combining requirements to contact separation time and average velocity—and it is discussed how these are influenced by different fault current scenarios, grid voltages and relay times. Through a demonstration case, we exemplify that an optimal actuator design features a trade-off between velocity and contact separation time.

title: Time-Resolved Travelling-Wave Protection Scheme for Monopolar DC Submarine Observatory Networks With Fault-Induced Communication Loss
abstract: Cable faults usually coincide with communication failures between branch units (BUs) and measurement loss near the fault point in submarine observatory networks, compromising protection reliability. This paper proposes a novel time-resolved protection scheme that integrates two traveling-wave temporal features: the extremum time captured at a single end and the multi-terminal wave arrival time differentials. This approach significantly reduces dependence on fault-prone communication links and measurement devices. An equivalent boundary impedance model is established to characterize traveling-wave behavior under grounding faults. The impacts of fault resistance, and fault location on the extremum time are analyzed. It is demonstrated that the extremum time is strongly correlated with the number of BUs traversed by the refraction wave, enabling accurate faulted cable identification. A selection strategy for protection installation locations is proposed, guided by redundancy requirements and traveling-wave detectability. Simulation results conducted on the NEPTUNE submarine observatory network using PSCAD/EMTDC demonstrate that the travelling-wave extremum time based scheme can rapidly isolate DC faults. Moreover, the multi-terminal traveling-wave method enhances protection redundancy, ensuring reliable operation even under partial measurement failure.

title: Error Characterization and Correction of a Simple Circuit Model for Accurate and Rapid Resonant Frequency Estimation in Traction Power Supply Systems
abstract: Harmonic resonance phenomena that arise in traction power supply systems (TPSS) can lead to severe operational consequences. Accurate determination of the resonant frequency in TPSS is essential for developing and implementing effective countermeasures to mitigate resonance risks. Existing estimation methods, including simple model-based calculations, high-fidelity simulation methods, operational data-driven identification strategies, and active harmonic injection techniques, each suffer from inherent limitations and none offers a solution that combines high accuracy, simplified modeling, and practical applicability. This article proposes a rapid estimation method for the resonant frequency based on a simplified circuit model. Quantitative analysis reveals considerable discrepancies between estimated resonant frequency and its reference, caused by round-off error during analytical derivations. Sensitivity analysis is performed to identify the key parameters influencing estimation accuracy. By bounding these parameters within reasonable ranges, the minimum expansion order required to limit approximation errors is determined. Correction coefficients are defined and precomputed to refine the initial estimation. Validation through comparisons with field measurements from TPSS and high-fidelity simulation results demonstrates that the proposed method enables accurate resonant frequency estimation.

title: Investigation of Metal Particles Behavior in the Interruption of Vacuum Switches
abstract: Late breakdown (LB) following interruption has become a critical limitation to the interruption performance of high-voltage (HV) vacuum interrupters (VIs), with metal particles widely considered as a primary key factor. To investigate the particle behavior in-depth during the interruption process, an optical diagnostic platform was developed to observe the metal particles throughout the entire interruption including arcing and post-arc stages. The particle formation under various electrode erosion modes were comprehensively investigated, and their post-arc motion was analyzed through trajectory tracking. Results show that for axial magnetic field (AMF) electrodes, moderately large currents below the rated short-circuit level can trigger intense cathodic activity, leading to abundant metal particles emission from the molten cathode surface, while the anode remains passive. After the current zero (CZ), once emitted particles collide with the contact surface, the cathode spot particles tend to rebound within the gap or off the chamber wall, while molten pool particles are often reabsorbed by the molten electrode surface. Both types of particles can persist in the gap long after CZ. The combined influence of these cathode particles may act as a primary trigger for LB. This study establishes the correlation between interrupting current, cathode activity, and metal particle generation, along with a detailed characterization of their spatiotemporal behavior during the entire interruption.

title: Dynamic Modeling of Tree-related High-impedance Faults Under Sustained Contact Conditions in Distribution Systems
abstract: Tree-related high-impedance faults (THIFs) represent a critical risk source for wildfires and power outages in distribution systems. Existing HIF models do not jointly consider the time-varying resistance of trees and the controllable nonlinear behavior of arcs. Consequently, they cannot support fault characteristic analysis across all time scales, thereby limiting the research and validation of THIF identification algorithms. To address this limitation, this paper presents a dynamic model for THIFs under sustained contact conditions that accurately characterizes fault currents over multiple time scales. First, extensive THIF experiments elucidate the failure mechanism and the evolution of current-waveform distortion characteristics. A piecewise-linear function is employed to represent the time varying electrical resistance of trees. Based on arc thermal equilibrium theory, a THIF arc model with controllable distortion characteristics is proposed, enabling independent regulation of current waveform distortion features through three physically meaningful parameters. This model can reproduce the envelope variations of fault currents over extended time scales and demonstrates superior fitting accuracy for local distortions within short time windows compared to existing models, significantly enhancing the ability to characterize THIF current behavior. Parameter ranges for the model's key variables are established from extensive experimental data, and the model serves as a reference for THIF inversion in simulations without actual measurement data. These findings provide a modeling foundation for early identification and intelligent detection of THIF in distribution systems, as well as for wildfire risk assessment.

title: Four-Leg Voltage Source Converter With Independent Phase Control for Ground Fault Compensation
abstract: Electrical faults are a frequent occurrence in medium voltage (MV) distribution grids, often affecting or completely interrupting the electrical supply. Among these, single-phase faults are the most common type and passive elements such as Peterson coils have been traditionally employed to mitigate their impact and maintain a reliable power supply. However, these solutions come with inherent drawbacks, including limited flexibility and functionality, which hinder their effectiveness in dynamic grid scenarios. This work presents a novel system designed to ensure high-quality power supply continuity before, during, and after single-phase faults. The proposed approach uses already installed four-leg power converters in the grid, eliminating the need for additional passive equipment. A new control strategy is developed in the natural $abc$ reference frame, which enables the use of classical control techniques in the MIMO system and simplifies the analysis of the output voltage loops without changing the reference frame. Simulations and experimental results confirm that the proposed control framework effectively compensates for faults and maintains grid stability, improving fault resilience in MV distribution networks.

title: Prior Knowledge-Guided Active Learning Network for Multi-Source Partial Discharge Diagnosis in Gas-Insulated Switchgear
abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence presents both opportunities and significant challenges for multi-source partial discharge (PD) diagnosis in gas-insulated switchgear (GIS), but challenges remain due to insufficient incorporation of underlying physical mechanisms, limited labeled data, noise interference, class imbalance, and difficulties in decoupling mixed PD sources. To address these issues, this paper proposes a prior knowledge–guided active learning network (PKGALN) for multi-source PD diagnosis in GIS, in which physics-related PD characteristics are explicitly embedded into the model design under a limited-label regime. Specifically, a prior knowledge–guided U-former is constructed by incorporating physically interpretable PD descriptors (e.g., time–frequency statistical features reflecting discharge behavior) as global guidance for feature learning, while a scale-guided convolutional–wavelet encoder enhances denoising and multi-scale representation capability. In addition, a multi-label decoupling recognition module is designed to explicitly handle mixed PD sources, and a distribution-balanced loss is adopted to alleviate severe class imbalance. To further reduce annotation cost, an adaptive active learning strategy is introduced, dynamically balancing uncertainty and diversity during sample selection. Experimental results on both laboratory and field datasets demonstrate that PKGALN achieves diagnostic accuracies of 96.39% and 93.26%, respectively, using only 10% of labeled samples. By leveraging limited labeled data, the proposed approach enables robust diagnosis of both single-source and multi-source PDs.

title: Analysis and Suppression of Overvoltage Caused by Catenary Fault Clearance in Flexible DC Traction Power Systems
abstract: Catenary faults in flexible DC traction power systems (FTPS) pose severe challenges to device safety and system stability due to overvoltage caused by fault clearance. This paper focuses on modeling, analysis and suppression of such overvoltage. Detailed modeling is conducted for successive overvoltage stages: preparation stage, development stage and recovery stage. Preparation stage affects the initial value. During development stage, fundamental cause of overvoltage is the shift in feeder current path, which is from injection into the fault point to injection into VSC capacitor, triggered by disconnection of the fault section. Recovery stage involves oscillation induced by RLC path. For overvoltage analysis, the decoupling of various factors such as source, grid and circuit breakers is achieved by constructing multiple cases through simulation. Finally, suppression methods including applying the Crowbar circuit and unblocking VSC in advance as well as adopting the outer-loop switching control strategy can effectively avoid reverse current entering capacitor so as to cause severe overvoltage. Combined methods can reduce the portion exceeding the normal voltage to around 1/3 of that without measures. The research on overvoltage in this paper is conducive to the design of new control and protection strategies for FTPS.

title: Fault Diagnosis Method for Single-Phase-to-Ground Faults Based on Phase-to-Phase Current Fault Components in Distribution Networks
abstract: Accurate diagnosis of single-phase-to-ground (SPG) faults in distribution networks is essential for rapid fault isolation and reduced power interruptions. Existing approaches often address only one aspect of fault diagnosis, suffering from low reliability, heavy communication requirements, and high investment costs. To overcome these challenges, this paper presents a comprehensive fault diagnosis method based on phase-to-phase current fault components (PPCFC). The fault characteristics of PPCFCs are firstly analyzed on both the substation and feeder sides, taking into account the practical configuration of current detection devices. The results show that, in faulty feeders and sections, the fault-phase-related PPCFCs are significantly larger than the healthy-phase-related ones, while in healthy feeders and sound sections, all three PPCFCs remain close to zero. The PPCFCs are then calculated with consideration of possible triggering delays under high impedance faults, and their amplitude features are extracted. Based on this analysis, a fault phase and faulty feeder identification method is developed using PPCFCs from a single feeder at the substation side. In addition, a distributed location strategy is proposed, which employs local indicators to accurately determine the fault section via simple binary communication. Extensive experiments confirm its effectiveness and practicality.

title: Resilience-Oriented Allocation of FI and RCS Considering Multi-Stage Collaborative Restoration With Improved Integer L-Shaped Method
abstract: Extreme disasters pose significant threats to distribution networks. While the allocation of Fault Indicators (FIs) and Sectionalizing Switches (SSs) can mitigate these impacts by accelerating fault localization and isolation, widespread deployment is often constrained by limited budgets. To address this, this paper proposes a resilience-oriented joint allocation optimization method for FIs and Remote Control Switches (RCSs). A two-stage stochastic programming model is constructed with the objective of minimizing the Expected Energy Not Served (EENS). This model comprehensively incorporates the time-sequence of multiple faults, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) patrolling strategies, and collaborative restoration measures involving fault isolation and repair crews. To efficiently handle the integer variables within the optimization, an improved integer L-shaped method is employed. The effectiveness of the proposed method is verified on a modified IEEE-123 system.

title: Fully Actuated Control of Point-to-Point VSC–HVDC Links for Frequency and DC Voltage Regulation in Asynchronous AC Systems
abstract: Grid-forming (GFM) VSC–HVDC systems can provide frequency support to ac grids, particularly in point-to point VSC–HVDC links interconnecting asynchronous ac systems. However, large power variations commanded for frequency support may jeopardize the dc-link voltage stability. To simultaneously enhance frequency support and preserve dc-link voltage regulation, this paper develops two robust controllers for the rectifier and inverter stations based on the fully actuated control (FAC) theory. FAC provides a systematic diffeomorphism-based transformation that converts the original under-actuated and strongly coupled station dynamics into an equivalent fully actuated form, thereby revealing virtual input channels and enabling direct shaping of the key dc-voltage- and frequency-related states for controller synthesis. In the transformed coordinates, multiple perturbations—including stochastic load variations, parameter uncertainties, and external disturbances—are aggregated as lumped disturbances. High-gain disturbance observers are then designed for both stations to estimate the lumped disturbances. Leveraging the observer-based estimates, a robust sliding-mode control law is formulated in the fully actuated coordinates to compensate the aggregated uncertainties, thereby ensuring resilient frequency support while maintaining dc-link voltage regulation. Simulation studies on two test systems validate the effectiveness of the proposed controllers in regulating the dc-link voltage and supporting grid frequency under multiple scenarios.

title: Autonomous Optimal Control for Wind Farm Integrated MMC-HVDC System Under Sending-End Single-Phase to Ground Fault
abstract: The integration of large-scale wind farm (WF) with modular multilevel converter-based high-voltage direct current (MMC-HVDC) systems is promising. However, this integration is challenged by the single-phase-to-ground (SLG) fault at sendingend overhead transmission lines. Existing SLG fault ride-through (FRT) strategies mainly focus on the fault stresses suppression and transient stability improvement. Less attention is paid to the grid voltage unbalance issue and the limited power transfer capability during SLG FRT. To address these issues, this paper proposes an autonomous optimal control (AOC) to enhance the SLG FRT performance. Firstly, considering the long-distance communication delays, autonomous optimization models are respectively established for MMC and WF, where MMC targets to maximize the power transmission while the WF aims to minimize the grid voltage unbalance. Secondly, with semi-definite relaxation (SDR) and second-order cone relaxation (SOCR), the original nonlinear nonconvex optimization models are transformed into computationally tractable convex formulations. Finally, the autonomous optimization models of MMC and WF are independently solved merely based on local measurements, the solutions of which are taken as the control reference during SLG FRT. Compared with the existing SLG FRT control, the proposed AOC can guarantee the maximum transmission of active power for MMC and minimum grid voltage unbalance for WF. Experimental results verify the effectiveness of the proposed AOC.

title: Monitoring Leakage Current in Insulator Strings for Flashover Risk Prediction: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: The accumulation of pollution on high-voltage insulators, combined with humidity, forms a conductive layer that drives leakage current (LC) activity, potentially leading to critical flashover events. This work presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) designed not only to map the current state of sensing technologies but to characterize the ongoing technological disruption in predictive maintenance. Analyzing 31 primary studies selected from 3939 records, this review identifies a paradigm shift from traditional statistical indicators to advanced Deep Learning (DL) architectures. Quantitative analysis reveals that modern pulse-based monitoring and DL approaches achieve prediction accuracies exceeding 98% in real-time scenarios, while hybrid multimodal frameworks (e.g., CNN-LSTM fused with climatic data) reach up to 99.2% in risk classification. Beyond synthesizing current benchmarks, this work contributes by translating research gaps into concrete technical directions for next-generation systems. These proposed directions include: (1) the application of Generative AI (GANs and Diffusion Models) to synthesize rare fault data and mitigate class imbalance; (2) the transition from standard RNNs to Transformers and xLSTM architectures for capturing long-term pollution trends; (3) the deployment of TinyML for edge-intelligence and online learning; and (4) the use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for optimizing sensor placement in transmission topologies. This study serves as a technical roadmap for implementing resilient, AI-driven insulator monitoring systems.

title: Automated Inverter-Embedded Testing of Step-Up Transformers in Renewable Energy Systems
abstract: Transformers are employed in renewable energy systems such as wind and solar power generation for stepping up the voltage supplied to the grid. They are known to have higher failure rates compared to grid transformers, as they are exposed to a hostile environment and fluctuating operating conditions. However, testing relies on on-site tests, which are costly to perform as they are installed in remote locations that are difficult to access. In this paper, a new approach for transformer testing using the inverter available in the system, is proposed. The main idea is to use the inverter as the test equipment for injecting test signals into the transformer low voltage (LV) winding to obtain the frequency response of admittance for detecting faults whenever the renewable energy system is de-energized. An equivalent circuit analysis is given to show that defects in the core, winding, insulation, and LCL filter can be detected from the change in admittance over a wide frequency range, similar to frequency response analysis (FRA) commonly used for transformer testing. Experimental test results of the proposed method and FRA performed on a 380/690V, 15 kVA, 3 phase transformer are given under emulated core insulation failure, insulation contamination, and poor electrical contacts for validation.

title: Different-frequency Differential Protection Method of Adjustable Speed Hydro-Generating Unit Based on Fixed Characteristic Frequency Band
abstract: During the operation of Adjustable speed hydro-generating unit (ASHU), due to high speed and large centrifugal force, the rotor winding is easily squeezed and causes short-circuit fault. The development of a reliable protection scheme is imperative. As a new and potential method, the universality of different-frequency differential protection is still limited under wide speed operation conditions. Therefore, a rotor winding short-circuit protection method based on fixed characteristic frequency band is proposed in this paper. Firstly, the internal relationship between the harmonic characteristics of rotor current and slip rate in the case of winding short-circuit fault of ASHU is analyzed. On this basis, the construction method of different-frequency differential current protection criterion based on fixed characteristic frequency band is proposed. Furthermore, combined with the waveform of the dynamic simulation experiment, the Generalized S Transform (GST) is used to carry out time-frequency analysis. The feasibility of the construction approach of the protection criterion is verified. Finally, the experimental results show that the proposed protection method is suitable for the wide speed operation condition of ASHU. It can achieve fast action under rotor winding short-circuit fault (RWSF), and has high selectivity under stator winding short-circuit fault (SWSF), which can effectively avoid protection misoperation.

title: Input Admittance Shaping-based Active Islanding Detection Technique for Multi-inverter Microgrids
abstract: Deploying grid ancillary services through distributed energy resources (DERs) challenges islanding detection techniques (IDTs). Power regulations, for instance, may mitigate power mismatches in islanded microgrids, increasing the risk of undetected islands. Additionally, when the grid is connected, false islanding detection during low-voltage events can disrupt low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) operations. Existing IDTs that comply with these services and requirements often suffer from power quality degradation and limited scalability in multi-inverter systems. To address these gaps, this study proposes an active IDT using the DER's input admittance shaping within a narrow negative-sequence frequency band. The shaped admittance results in a negligible negative-sequence disturbance (NSD) injection during grid-connected operation while ensuring rapid and synchronized NSD jump after island formation in multi-inverter systems. Thus, islanding is detected when the rate of change of negative-sequence voltage at the DER terminal exceeds a preset threshold within a specified timeframe. Importantly, the proposed IDT does not affect the positive sequence component, avoiding conflict with ancillary services in grid-connected operations. Numerous simulations are conducted in PSCAD-EMTDC in accordance with the IEEE Std. 1547.1-2020 test procedure. The results demonstrate precise and rapid islanding detection in single- and multi-inverter scenarios, including zero/small power mismatches with DER's power regulations. In addition, the proposed IDT does not exhibit false tripping during low-voltage events, complying with LVRT requirements.

title: Calculation of Positive-Sequence and Zero-Sequence Impedances of Three-Phase Submarine Cables
abstract: This paper describes semi-analytical calculation methods for the positive-sequence and zero-sequence impedances of 3-phase armored cables with solid sheaths and a single armor layer. Separate equivalent circuits are defined for these two impedances. Subsequently, circuit component values are calculated based on 2D field equations, with some 3D effects modeled. The existing approach for calculating zero-sequence impedance is corrected and expanded by inclusion of additional inductances due to solenoidal fields and magnetic armor effects. 3D finite-element models of cables with magnetic and non-magnetic armor are used to assess the accuracy of our circuit models; discrepancies are less than 3% at frequencies between 50 Hz and 5 kHz. Python code with the implementation of the method is provided for accessibility.

title: Reduction of Arc-Induced Mechanical Stress on a 1000 kV Power Transformer Tank through Embedded High-Voltage Lead Exit Design
abstract: The high-voltage lead exit is installed in a compact turret external to a 1000 kV power transformer tank. Strong shock waves induced by high-energy arc faults in the lead exit pose a serious risk to turret and tank safety. To enhance the arc withstand capability of 1000 kV power transformer tanks, this study proposes a novel embedded high-voltage lead exit design. Compared to traditional configurations, the enlarged embedded lead exit facilitates the dispersion and attenuation of arc-induced pressure waves, thereby reducing the risk of explosion and combustion. A comprehensive evaluation—including electric field distribution, mechanical strength, and explosion resistance —is conducted to validate the structural reliability and arc fault tolerance of the proposed design. Notably, an arc pressure simulation method based on the bubble pulsation approach is introduced, in which actual arc power is injected into a gas volume equivalent to the arc length to model the pressure source. The Johnson–Cook (JC) failure criterion is employed to accurately evaluate material failure. Simulation results confirm that the embedded configuration significantly enhances arc fault resistance under various internal fault scenarios. This novel design offers a practical solution for improving the safety and reliability of ultra-high-voltage (UHV) transformers and provides valuable insights for optimizing high-voltage lead exit structures in critical applications.

title: Graph Theory-Based Topology Derivation for Multifunctional DC Choppers of a DFIG
abstract: As critical protection devices for achieving low-voltage ride-through (LVRT) in a doubly-fed induction generator (DFIG), DC choppers are widely used because of their low costs and high reliability. The conventional DC choppers are limited to DC-link voltage regulation and cannot provide rotor current control. This inherent limitation has spurred growing research interest in multifunctional DC choppers (MDCCs). However, the absence of a systematic approach for deriving the topologies of MDCCs has significantly constrained their practical applications, resulting in only a limited number of proposed configurations. To address this challenge, in this study, a systematic topology derivation methodology for MDCCs is proposed. The hierarchical three-stage topology derivation method sequentially generates unweighted, weighted, and directed-weighted graphs. Moreover, the specific characteristics of an MDCC are modeled via formally established topology filtering criteria, which ensures the completeness of the generation process. The proposed code-implemented method significantly improves the efficiency of MDCC design while maintaining high configuration accuracy. A hardware-in-the-loop experimental validation conducted on a real-time digital simulator (RTDS) confirms that the optimized topology (with only two insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs), two diodes and one resistor) achieves satisfactory performance during LVRT transients.

title: Transmission Line Galloping Detection System Based on an Improved PIDNet
abstract: The galloping phenomenon of transmission lines, exacerbated by extreme weather, poses a significant threat to grid stability and power supply. The practical application of conventional sensor-based methods is limited by high deployment costs and low adaptability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an end-to-end galloping detection system based on video monitoring. An improved PIDNet forms the segmentation backbone, incorporating a Line-features Interactive Two-Branch (LITB) network to leverage line orientation priors, a Detail Recovery Decoder (DRD) to enhance line continuity, and an Edge Perception Module (EPM) to refine boundary segmentation against complex backgrounds. Optical flow analysis is subsequently employed to quantify transmission line displacement and determine galloping states. Experimental results demonstrate performance improvements of 6.9% in mIoU, 4.23% in mAcc, and 4.8% mDice over popular segmentation models. The proposed embedded detection system achieves an accuracy of 84.00%, a recall of 90.31%, and an F1-score of 87.17% when deployed on edge devices.

title: Analytical Model of Capacitive Voltage Transformers for the Calculation of Voltage Collapse Transients
abstract: Protection relays monitor system voltage through Capacitive Voltage Transformers (CVTs), which scale voltages to safe levels. However, during voltage collapse, CVTs lag in transmitting the event due to their internal capacitors, impairing protection performance. Because of this, manufacturers and relay operators need an accessible, simple and reliable model to design and predict CVT behavior under collapse conditions. This paper presents an analytical model of CVT transient response during voltage collapse. The proposed model is validated against an established Electromagnetic Transient (EMT) simulation tool. Our model predicts the output voltage under sustained short circuits at the input without simulations, eliminating the need for specialized software or extensive training. Derived from an accepted equivalent circuit, it depends only on CVT parameters and construction. The model applies across wide burden ranges, accuracy classes, and several ferroresonance suppression circuit types (resistive, electronic, or non-linear). Compared with EMT simulations, the model achieves over 90% accuracy and dependability across all tested cases. The model can be readily integrated into CVT design workflows using standard software, enabling faster and more economical modeling of CVT behavior during voltage collapse tests as required by industry standards.

title: Optimum Coordination of Overcurrent Relays in Electrical Power Distribution Networks using the Generalized Reduced Gradient Method
abstract: The protection system in the electrical power distribution networks is essential to guarantee the safety and efficiency of the electrical energy supply. Coordinating and optimizing the operation of protection devices is a complex problem, whose objective aims to guarantee adequate detection and isolation of faults, minimizing interruptions and ensuring network stability. Some techniques have been applied for optimal coordination including heuristic methods, metaheuristics and linearized models. These techniques have limitations, i.e., do not guarantee good quality solutions and simplify the problem by reducing the number of variables. This work proposes a deterministic mathematical optimization model with application of iterative nonlinear programming techniques, using the generalized reduced gradient method (GRG), to find good quality solutions for the proper coordination and selectivity of overcurrent relays (OCR). A comparative analysis is conducted between the proposed methodology and a genetic algorithm (metaheuristic approach) by assessing their solution quality, computational efficiency, and robustness. The obtained results demonstrate several advantages of using the GRG, that include better coordination and selectivity of OCRs, computational tractability and a faster response of the protection system.

title: Prediction Method for Audible Noise of High-Altitude Extra-High Voltage AC Transmission Lines Based on Long-Term Observations
abstract: Audible noise (AN) is a critical parameter in the economic and environmental design of extra-high voltage (EHV) AC transmission lines, especially in high-altitude regions. Although several altitude correction factors and AN prediction methods have been proposed based on corona cage tests and long-term observations, the accuracy remains uncertain owing to the limited measurement data from high-altitude transmission lines. This study addresses this gap through long-term observations of four EHV transmission lines on the Tibetan Plateau, combined with existing corona cage test results. The cumulative distribution of AN in rainy weather was obtained from various observation stations. By comparing measured values from stations at different altitudes and combining the experimental results from a movable corona cage, an altitude correction method for AN was developed. Subsequently, by comparing statistical data from four high-altitude observation stations with predicted results from different approaches, the predicted values were found to be overestimated. An improved prediction method for AN in rainy weather was proposed. Additionally, based on the statistical differences observed over one year at multiple long-term observation stations, a method for evaluating AN under varying weather conditions was investigated. A predictive model for AN under different rainfall conditions was developed based on correlation and multiple regression analyses, and its accuracy was validated. The findings of this study provide a crucial reference for the prediction and evaluation of AN from EHV AC transmission lines in high-altitude regions.

title: Sequence-Impedance-Based Interactions Analysis of a VSG with Dynamic and Constant-Power Loads at Varying Grid Strength Conditions
abstract: Induction motor loads (IMLs) and constant-power loads (CPLs) are common in commercial and industrial load environments, underscoring the importance of understanding their impact on modern converter-based power systems. This paper characterizes the dynamic interactions of a grid-forming converter controlled as a virtual synchronous generator (VSG) with local IML and CPL under varying grid strength conditions. Analytical sequence impedance models for the VSG, IML, and CPL are developed to represent their dynamic behavior and to examine VSG-load-grid interactions using frequency response and Nyquist stability criterion analyses. The study reveals that an IML degrades the dynamic performance of the VSG, introducing low frequency oscillations under weak-grid conditions and potentially causing instability as the short-circuit ratio increases. The CPL, in contrast, enhances the VSG dynamics at low and high short-circuit ratios. Moreover, when coexisting with an IML in a VSG-IML CPL grid system, a CPL can enhance oscillation damping, broaden the range of stable control parameters, improve system dynamics during grid disturbances, and restore system stability at higher short-circuit ratios. The theoretical findings are validated through detailed nonlinear-model time-domain simulations.

title: An Analytical Investigation on Selection of I-APF and R-APF to Mitigate Harmonic Resonance in HVDC Terminal Under Capacity Constraints
abstract: With the rapid advancement of power electronics, active power filters (APFs) have emerged as a preferred solution for mitigating harmonic resonance in high-voltage direct current (HVDC) systems. APFs can be broadly categorized into current compensation APFs (I-APFs) and resistive APFs (R-APFs), depending on their control strategies. Although both types have demonstrated effectiveness in practical applications, previous studies have not comprehensively compared their resonance mitigation performance, particularly under capacity-limited conditions. To address this gap, this paper establishes an equivalent harmonic model for LCC-HVDC systems with APFs connected and proposes a novel metric, capacity utilization efficiency (CUE), to compare the resonance suppression effectiveness of APFs. The variation characteristics of CUE are systematically analyzed considering factors such as resonance frequency, system damping, and APF capacity. The findings provide a practical guideline to assist utilities in selecting the optimal APF control, accounting for factors such as varying network impedances and background harmonic distortions. Finally, the developed harmonic model and the APF-selection guideline are validated using a real-life LCC-HVDC system experiencing resonance issues and a modified IEEE 39-bus system.

title: System-Wide Instrument Transformer Calibration and Line Parameter Estimation Using PMU Data
abstract: Uncalibrated instrument transformers (ITs) can degrade the performance of downstream applications that rely on the voltage and current measurements that ITs provide. It is also well-known that phasor measurement unit (PMU)-based system-wide IT calibration and line parameter estimation (LPE) are interdependent problems. In this paper, we present a statistical framework for solving the simultaneous LPE and IT calibration (SLIC) problem using synchrophasor data. The proposed approach not only avoids the need for a “perfect” IT by judiciously placing a revenue quality meter (which is an expensive but non-perfect IT), but also accounts for the variations typically occurring in the line parameters. The results obtained using multiple IEEE test systems as well as actual power system data demonstrate the high accuracy, robustness, and practical utility of the proposed approach.

title: A Mixed-Frequency Modulation Based Four-Port Soft Open Point with Three 10 kV/3 MW AC Ports and One ±10 kV/1 MW DC Port
abstract: A mixed-frequency modulation based four-port soft open point (MF-SOP) is proposed and implemented for medium voltage distribution network. The MF-SOP consists of three 10 kV/ 3 MW ac ports and one ±10 kV/ 1 MW dc port, enabling the management of power flow among multiple ac feeders and the dc bus. The mixed-frequency modulation method is adopted and resonant paths are constructed. In this paper, the key parameters are designed considering the effect of mixed-frequency voltage and current. Due to the characteristics of the mixed-frequency modulation method, the traditional grounding method cannot be applied directly. This paper explores the grounding issues and grounding method for mixed-frequency based multiport converters. In addition, a compact startup circuit is proposed and the corresponding startup process is devised. Finally, long-term power tests demonstrate the reliability and stability of proposed MF-SOP. To the author's knowledge, the proposed MF-SOP represents the first practical application of mixed-frequency modulation technology in flexible interconnection project. The power density exceeds 0.101 MW/m³ and the peak efficiency above 98.69%.

title: Generalized Neural Network to Locate Fault in DC Microgrid Using Limited Initial Samples
abstract: High discharge rate of the DC link capacitor during a line fault in a DC microgrid causes a steep rise in the line fault current. Previous line fault detection techniques typically detect a low resistance fault in DC microgrids within a few microseconds; therefore, a fault location estimation scheme using a few initial samples is necessary. This work proposes a local-measurement-based offline fault location estimation scheme using a few initial samples. The proposed generalized approach aims to obtain an optimal Neural Network (NN) to predict the fault location in DC microgrids for each input data set. The proposed scheme is validated for initial samples ($=2$ and 4), making the location estimation time $120\mu$s and $240\mu$s, respectively, with $60\mu$ s sampling time. The estimation accuracy is further refined by averaging each prediction as the ultimate fault location. The proposed scheme is validated using the Real-Time Digital Simulator on a 400 V DC microgrid with different operating modes. Parallel assessment with previous techniques and comparison with traditional NN shows the superiority of the proposed scheme in fault location estimation with a few initial samples.

title: Critical End-Effect at Sea-to-Land Transition of Three Core Submarine Cables
abstract: At the sea-to-land transition or offshore interfaces, three-core submarine cables are separated into individual single-core cables arranged in a flat configuration. This separation, combined with protective layers over metallic sheaths that impart semiconductive properties and cause spatial bonding, results in localized increases in circulating sheath currents in the submarine portion of the installation. Despite potential thermal consequences in offshore cable projects, this specific issue has received limited attention in the existing literature; consequently, this paper presents a novel examination of this end-effect phenomenon. An analytical model is developed in the paper and cross-validated with a comprehensive three-dimensional Finite Element Method (FEM) model and PI-section simulations, which represent fundamentally different approaches. The study addresses practical mitigation strategies for end effects in submarine cable installations and addresses a critical gap in existing methods for rating calculations of submarine power cables.

title: A Non-Unit DC Line Protection Based on Extremum Time of Fault Forward Traveling Wave
abstract: Compared with the traditional derivative-based traveling wave (TW) protection, the non-unit TW protection based on fault TW waveform analysis can effectively enhance sensitivity when high-resistance faults occur. However, protection based on fault TW waveform analysis may operate incorrectly due to inaccurate characterization of the initial fault TW, as well as the influence of subsequent TWs under line-port faults and the fault resistance associated with external faults. To address this issue, a non-unit DC line protection based on the extremum time of forward TW is proposed. Specifically, the differences in initial fault TWs associated with different fault locations are fully considered, together with the influences of fault resistance and subsequent TWs on waveform characteristics. The distinctions among different fault locations are then captured through criteria based on the extremum time of the forward TW and the fault voltage amplitude. Therefore, the proposed protection can effectively detect internal line-port and remote faults. The detailed model of the modular multilevel converter-based high voltage direct current (MMC-HVDC) transmission system is built in Real Time Digital Simulator (RTDS), and the proposed protection algorithm is programmed in the DC protection device. Hardware-in-the-loop test and simulation results show that this protection method can effectively address the problem of protection refusal under line-port or remote fault, and can withstand 400Ω transition resistance and noise with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 30dB.

title: Research on the Diagnosis and Localization Method of Cross-Bonding Cable Defects Based on Three-Phase Differential Frequency Excitation
abstract: In high-voltage network, long-distance cables use cross bonding (CB) to eliminate the sheath currents and ensure the stable operation of the power system. Existing impedance testing suffers from signal attenuation and distortion due to limited instrument output, while cross-bonding causes phase coupling and signal aliasing, which interfere with defect diagnosis and localization accuracy. These combined factors affect the accuracy of defect localization for the cables. This paper proposes a method for diagnosing and locating defects in cross-bonding cables based on three-phase differential frequency excitation. An equivalent CB cable model was constructed to analyze the relationship between defects and resonant frequency shifts. A CB cable impedance spectrum analysis method was constructed, utilizing small frequency differences and fundamental frequency information to achieve full coverage of defect information for three single-phase cables in the wide frequency range. A testing system is built to obtain impedance spectra for damaged and thermally aged cables. Based on the offset characteristics of peak frequencies, the identification of defect types was achieved. Defect types are identified based on peak frequency offsets, and a differential frequency localization function is used to locate defects with an accuracy of 0.1%, verifying the effectiveness of the method.

title: MFT-NNLS: A Toolbox For Passive Macromodeling From Large Immittance and Scattering Data Sets Using Vector Fitting And Residue Perturbation in Matlab
abstract: This paper describes a Matlab toolbox (MFT-NNLS) for passive macromodeling of large-scale problems defined by admittance, impedance or scattering data in the frequency domain. Vector Fitting (VF) is used for calculating an initial rational model having a common pole set. Passivity can afterwards be enforced by residue perturbation of the associated pole-residue model. Highly efficient implementations are utilized, including the so-called fast implementation of VF, and passivity enforcement with problem compacting via the QR-NNLS method with usage of a fast LU-based non-negative least squares solver. The final result is a rational model satisfying the physical conditions of realness, stability, passivity and reciprocity. The rational model is returned on alternative forms, including a pole-residue model and a state-space model with real-valued or complex-valued parameters. Optional parameters are available for tuning the behavior of the software to the given application, e.g., least squares weighting schemes and alternative methods for passivity assessment. Model export to leading electromagnetic transient programs is included. Several applications are shown, including large-scale problems from high-voltage power systems (high orders, many terminals) and high-speed electronics (many ports). The software consists of a collection of Matlab functions.

title: A Service Restoration Methodology for Active Distribution Network Based on Joint Robust Optimization of Mobile Energy Storage and Islanding
abstract: Mobile energy storage (MES) with flexible regulation and dynamic transfer capabilities can provide proactive support to facilitate the safe operation of active distribution networks (ADN). To address the challenge of emergency power supply during extreme events, a novel service restoration method for ADN is proposed, which considers the joint robust optimization of islanding power supply and MES scheduling with repair crews. First, the Davidson-Webert-Akcelik traffic impedance combination function is proposed based on the mapping relationship between MES stations and roadway nodes. This function analyzes the roadway conditions of MES under an extreme event by highlighting the flexibility of MES as an emergency power source in ADN service restoration. Second, A Boolean variable-based load outage time model is established to quantify multiple switching operations of loads under power balance constraints in the service restoration. Third, a robust optimization model for islanding and MES considering roads and lines repair crews is proposed to improve ADN service restoration capability, where road repair crews (RRCs) restore road to enhance MES mobility, and line repair crews (LRCs) repair power lines to reduce MES power demand. The solution can be obtained through interactive iterative optimization using the Column and Constraint Generation (C&CG) algorithm. Finally, the coupling system including modified IEEE 33-node system and 17-node road network is simulated to demonstrate the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed method.

title: Transient Model of Grounding System Considering Soil Ionization and Frequency-Dependent Electrical Parameters
abstract: Lightning strikes are a leading cause of power outages in transmission systems. Evaluating the transient response of grounding systems is critical for effective lightning protection. This response is governed by both soil ionization and frequency-dependent properties. Previous studies often faced challenges in accurately modeling soil ionization and validations limited to experimental currents featuring either short wavefronts or high amplitudes. This paper proposes a transient model for a grid-type grounding system that accounts for both soil ionization and frequency-dependent effects, solved using a Fourier transform-based time-frequency domain transformation method. By integrating layered soil modeling with an electric field-dependent soil ionization model, the approach significantly enhances computational accuracy. The model is validated under triggered lightning conditions considering a soil resistivity of 230 Ω·m, and effectively addresses both short wavefronts and high-amplitude currents, with model predictions deviating from measurements by only 3.5%.

title: SHAP-Based Interpretable Neural Network Framework for Lightning Risk Analysis and Diagnosis in Power Transmission Lines
abstract: Although SHAP and other explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques have been applied in several power system scenarios, lightning protection strategies in transmission lines still rely heavily on the practical experience of operation and maintenance personnel. To address this gap, this study proposes a quantitative diagnostic framework based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to identify the root causes of high lightning risks. To facilitate the extensive computations required by SHAP, a dual-hidden-layer neural network is integrated as a surrogate model to efficiently approximate lightning trip rates. This framework is then applied to analyze the specific risk factors of transmission towers along a line in Yunnan Province, China. The results obtained using the SHAP method were also used to formulate targeted lightning protection measures for these towers, thereby effectively reducing their risks to a reasonable level. The quantitative weights derived using the SHAP method aligned well with theoretical principles of lightning trip rate calculations, validating the rationality and effectiveness of this method in diagnosing causes of lightning risks for transmission lines.

title: A Novel Criterion of Transient Stability Analysis for the Wind Power Grid-Connected System
abstract: The large-scale integration of new energy sources into the power grid leads to a low-inertia characteristic of the grid. This weakens the ability of the grid to regulate when disturbed and poses a severe risk of transient instability. Conventional methods of power system stability analysis face the limitation of being overly conservative. This paper adopts a manifold-based stability analysis method, combined with the distribution of singularities, to characterize the boundary of stability domain (BSD) of the system. The domain is mapped onto the unit sphere via central projection transformation, which offers a more intuitive representation of the domain. There is a contradiction between the size of the domain and the dynamic response speed; specifically, increasing the domain may reduce the dynamic response speed. In this paper, a novel criterion of transient stability analysis, namely the singularity invariance criterion (SIC) is proposed. This criterion enables dynamic adjustment of system parameters to avoid the contradiction. The IEEE 39 bus system simulation shows that under the same parameter variation conditions, the SIC-based method can increase TVI/% by 14.84% (BSD size index) and reduce RTVI/% (response speed index) by 14.93%, which is superior to the energy function method. This criterion provides a new theoretical basis for the stability analysis of grid-connected systems.
