title: Digital Twin Assisted Health Degradation Analysis and Control of Grid-Integrated PV Systems: Using UVISMC and EAAEFO Algorithm
abstract: This paper explores the use of Digital Twin (DT) technology for real-time health monitoring of grid-integrated photovoltaic (PV) systems. The proposed DT is developed through conceptualization, computational modeling, and experimental validation, functioning as a mathematical replica of the hardware system. Operating alongside the physical setup, the DT leverages measured sensor data to enable accurate tracking and control. A novel Power Law Charge Function-based Enhanced Adaptive Artificial Electric Field Optimization (EAAEFO) algorithm is employed to continuously compare DT outputs with real system measurements, ensuring precise analysis. For control, a Unit Vector Integrated Sliding Mode Control (UVISMC) scheme based on Cascaded Generalized Integrator (CGI) is introduced. This strategy provides improved current tracking, robustness, and reduced sensitivity to parameter variations compared to conventional controllers. The DT framework is implemented on the OPAL-RT (OP4512) platform, while the hardware prototype operates on an NI sbRIO-9636 FPGA board using LabVIEW. Health degradation of interfacing inductors, converter switches, and DC-link capacitors is examined by analyzing its impact on system performance. Experimental validation demonstrates that the DT achieves over 98% accuracy in replicating hardware behavior, even under degraded conditions, establishing its effectiveness for PV system monitoring and control.

title: Short-Duration Current Analysis for Predictive Aging Estimation in Power Transformer Insulation
abstract: The lifespan of power transformer insulation is significantly influenced by its Degree of Polymerization (DP), which reflects the average number of polymerized units in the cellulose chains of paper insulation. As cellulose forms the structural core of the insulation, its DP critically affects both mechanical integrity and electrical performance. Conventional methods for determining DP are invasive and require physical sampling, rendering them unsuitable for in-service transformers. This study presents a non-invasive, circuit-model-based approach to estimate DP using time-domain dielectric response data acquired over a short measurement interval (typically 25 seconds). The method utilizes the initial polarization current decay and its corresponding system response, which are modeled through a transfer function representation of the insulation system. A distinct correlation is observed between the early-time decay characteristics and the underlying DP of the insulation. The proposed technique has been validated on datasets obtained from multiple in-service power transformers. Results confirm that the approach can reliably extract DP-related parameters from short-duration dielectric signals, enabling practical, on-site condition assessment without interrupting transformer operation.

title: Prescribed Performance Voltage Regulation in Islanded Microgrids: An Event-Triggered Fault Compensation Approach
abstract: This paper addresses the voltage control and dynamic performance optimization of inverter-based distributed generation units in islanded microgrids. To tackle practical challenges such as system dynamic constraints, nonlinear characteristics, uncertain actuator faults, and limited communication resources, a distributed cooperative control strategy based on a multi-agent system is proposed. First, to strictly constrain the consensus error in the distributed control system, a barrier function configured with a hyperbolic sine function is designed. This ensures that the consensus error satisfies the preset performance constraints, thereby improving the controllability of the system’s dynamic evolution. Second, to address potential unknown actuator faults such as partial failure and bias misalignment, a second-order dynamic compensation signal is constructed and combined with an adaptive law to achieve real-time online estimation and rapid compensation of fault parameters. This significantly enhances the system’s fault tolerance and robustness. Finally, to reduce the communication burden in the distributed control system and effectively suppress grid harmonics and oscillations caused by abrupt changes in control commands, an event-triggered control mechanism with a decreasing threshold characteristic is introduced, saving communication resources for the microgrid. Theoretical analysis and simulation results verify the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed method.

title: Vibration-Based Detection of Cable Bending in Cable GIS Terminations via Experimental Measurements and Interface Stress Simulation
abstract: Cable GIS terminations are prone to insulation defects induced by abnormal internal stress and strain, due to their complex internal structure, latent defects, and sensitivity to installation quality. One typical manifestation of such abnormal mechanical states is internal cable bending, whose influence on the vibration response of cable GIS terminations remains insufficiently understood. To address this issue, this study proposes a vibration based method for detecting abnormal stress-strain conditions at insulation interfaces, enabling early identification of hidden insulation defects. First, vibration theory and simulation models are combined to examine how internal cable bending influences interfacial insulation pressure and the corresponding vibration response. Subsequently, a vibration testing platform for 110-kV cable GIS terminations is established to measure and analyze the vibration characteristics under normal and simulated abnormal stress-strain conditions, with the latter induced by cable bending. Finally, the vibration characteristics are evaluated using time domain and frequency-domain indicators. The results demonstrate that internal cable bending leads to non-uniform stress distributions at the insulation interfaces between the bushing, stress cone, and cable. The cable-end vibration, which is typically the most pronounced under normal conditions, is significantly suppressed, accompanied by a noticeable shift of the vibration signal toward the lower-frequency domain and an increase in damping. These findings establish a vibration response characterization framework for cable bending defects and provide a basis for non-intrusive condition assessment of cable GIS terminations.

title: Single-Ended Fault Location Method Based on Control Characteristics of Inverter-Based Resources for Low-Frequency Transmission System
abstract: Accurate fault location is crucial for power system emergency repair. However, the existing fault analysis-based fault location methods for the outgoing line of inverter-based resources use the traditional synchronous generator-based source model as the remote-end source model. The reliance on traditional source characteristics limits the adaptability of these methods in low-frequency transmission system (LFTS) used for offshore wind farm integration, where both ends of the system are inverter-based resources. Therefore, a novel fault location method is proposed for LFTS, which incorporates the source equations and fault network equations. Firstly, the source equations of LFTS are derived from control characteristics, while the network equations are derived from sequence networks and fault boundary conditions. Then, the fault location is converted into an optimization problem. The constraints of source equations, network equations and actual measured values are integrated in the objective functions, thereby allowing the fault distance and fault resistance to be identified by solving optimization problem. Finally, the performance of proposed fault location method is verified in PSCAD/EMTDC. The proposed fault location method exhibits an error of less than 1% in most cases, with a maximum error of less than 4%, and a fault resistance tolerability up to 300 Ω.

title: Design and Passivity Analysis of MMC-Based STATCOM With Active Harmonic Filtering
abstract: Power quality is a growing concern in modern electrical power systems due to the increasing penetration of power electronic interfaced nonlinear loads and generation, which introduce voltage and current distortions. Active filter techniques have been developed to mitigate these distortions. Among these techniques, virtual harmonic impedance is the most desired for harmonic power sharing or general power quality improvements. However, existing methods often lack explicit passivity considerations, which can lead to adverse interactions with the grid resonances. This paper presents a control design for a grid-forming Modular Multilevel Converter (MMC)-based STATCOM with virtual harmonic impedance. The proposed method enables the selection of a harmonic impedance that improves power quality while ensuring a positive passivity index around the converter harmonic admittance, thus guaranteeing stable interactions with the grid. This control approach is based on a dq-frame feed-forward harmonic compensator. The paper outlines the tuning methodology to achieve a harmonic virtual impedance, operational boundaries, and robustness of the proposed approach. Simulation results in a harmonic benchmark system demonstrate that the proposed control achieves the desired harmonic impedance while maintaining a passive response, ensuring stable system performance.

title: Probabilistic Multi-Objective Design of Lightning Protection for Complex Power Distribution Networks
abstract: Some of the main issues in developing an effective lightning protection strategy include determining the optimal placement of protection devices and deciding whether to incorporate shield wires. Addressing these challenges involves balancing multiple, often conflicting, objectives. Additionally, the intrinsic probabilistic nature of the lightning problem makes the optimization even more complicated. Based on the above considerations, this study proposes a multi-objective optimization framework to identify effective lightning protection strategies, in terms of surge arrester location and shield wire installation in complex distribution networks. The proposed approach aims to find a computationally efficient procedure that preserves the accuracy of conventional methods, even in complex network configurations. This is accomplished by integrating decision theory with a Design of Experiments approach based on Taguchi arrays to determine the optimal protection alternative. This method allows obtaining substantial reduction of the computational time. The computational time reduction depends on the network complexity and on the configuration of the reference method. In the simulations presented in this paper, the proposed approach allowed reducing computational time up to approximately 98% compared to a benchmark method based on genetic algorithm combined with the Monte Carlo technique, while preserving the accuracy of the results. The proposed method offers a practical and scalable solution for enhancing lightning resilience despite the complexity of the distribution networks' topology.

title: A 9–150 kHz Disturbances Measurement Method for Power Quality and Compatibility Levels
abstract: With the large-scale integration of new energy sources into power grids, the level of disturbances in new power systems has gradually increased. The disturbances in the 9–150 kHz frequency band may exceed the limit values of the electromagnetic compatibility in the IEC 61000-2-2 standard. However, methods for measuring disturbances in this band are still under development. Currently, IEC SC77A/WG9 is developing a quasi-peak (QP) measurement method of disturbances in the 9–150 kHz band for the IEC 61000-4-30 standard. Therefore, this paper proposes a 9–150 kHz QP measurement method (compressed sensing–phase-locked loop, CS-PLL method) that conforms to the framework of the IEC 61000-4-30 standard. The phase-locked loop (PLL) disturbance tracking part of the method enables disturbance tracking with less computation, whereas frequency pre-estimation effectively shortens the PLL method adaptation process and reduces the measurement uncertainty at short window lengths. After simulation and experimental signal verification, the combination of frequency pre-estimation and the PLL method can achieve a measurement uncertainty of less than 5% in a 200 ms QP measurement window. This meets the measurement window length proposal of the IEC 61000-4-30 standard framework and the measurement uncertainty proposal for this frequency band.

title: Distributed Acoustic Emission Detection Method for GIS Partial Discharge Based on Dual Mach–Zehnder Optical Fiber Interferometry
abstract: Currently, piezoelectric transducer (PZT) based sensing systems are the dominant method for detecting partial discharge (PD) via acoustic emission (AE) in gas-insulated switchgear (GIS). Nevertheless, standard PZT systems often struggle to satisfy the stringent operation and maintenance demands of contemporary power equipment. Numerous research teams have recently explored novel acoustic emission sensing technologies based on optical fiber interferometers. Despite these advances, most existing research has concentrated heavily on enhancing sensor sensitivity, often overlooking the potential for multiplexing. Consequently, true distributed sensing capabilities have not yet been fully realized. To address this gap, an acoustic emission detection method based on a dual Mach–Zehnder (DMZ) optical fiber interferometer is proposed in this paper. This method can not only detect high-frequency AE signals but also identify the AE source via the time difference of the arrival of signals at the two interferometers. The latter is crucial for realizing distributed acoustic emission detection of PD in GIS. Based on this methodology, key parameters for the DMZ optical fiber sensing system were designed, and an experimental platform was established to evaluate the response and localization performance of the sensing system. Furthermore, a PD detection experiment on a real 110 kV GIS was conducted to evaluate the detection ability of the system for metallic particle defects. Experimental validation demonstrates that the proposed DMZ sensing architecture can identify discharge events down to the hundreds of picocoulombs (pC) range. The system achieves a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) approximately 5 dB higher than that of conventional PZT systems. Additionally, the system supports the serial multiplexing of 20 sensing units and achieves a localization error of 6.6 m for the locus of the AE signal activity in the optical path.

title: A Unified Probability Model for Multi-type Power Quality Disturbances based on Operating States identification
abstract: The Grid-connected inverter (GCI) inevitably generates the multi-type power quality disturbances at the same time; for example, it not only emits harmonic currents but also causes voltage fluctuations. Building one model to describe the multi-type disturbances is necessary for disturbance source tracing, disturbance prediction, mitigation decision, and so on. This study proposes a unified probability model for multi-type power quality disturbances for GCI based on operating states identification. Firstly, it proposes an operating states identification algorithm considering multi-type disturbances, to facilitate the construction of the disturbance model for different operating states. Secondly, the unified probability model for multi-type power quality disturbances is developed, which includes the edge probability model and unified probability model, to analyze the occurrence probability and coupling relationship of multi-type disturbances. Finally, the accuracy and validity of the proposed method are verified by using the real recorded data of photovoltaic (PV) GCI in practice.

title: Assessing Maintenance of Medium Voltage Cable Networks Under Time-Varying Loading
abstract: The electrification and ongoing energy transition lead to systematic changes in electricity loading and variability in power systems. Distribution systems were designed for regular operating patterns, assuming constant low loading. Now, operators need to assess whether their assets can withstand more, as well as time-varying loading. Operating the system at or near its ampacity potentially accelerates thermal ageing, so the question arises: ‘how much can one operate at the limits while keeping maintenance and failures low?’ This paper introduces a novel approach that derives a time-varying Weibull approximation of failure rates using thermal models and provides a shortcut method to quantify maintenance implications under time-varying loading for heterogeneous MV cable populations. The case studies investigate a dataset from Denmark and the Oberrhein Medium Voltage (MV) system in Germany, studying ageing assets and the interplay with loading, and replacement paradigms of two different cable insulation types. The studies demonstrate that a small fraction of $25\%$ of old, low-quality cables leads to $82\%$ of failures, and $1.4\%$ of the time of highest loading can cause $46\%$ of cable ageing. The case studies also demonstrate that maintenance needs may be between $10-300$ times higher under future loading conditions associated with the energy transition, specifically in networks that have older PILC cables. This paper provides a new tool for operators to plan maintenance under more realistic, future operating conditions.

title: Evaluation Method for Intrusion Current in Urban Power Grid Caused by Metro Stray Current Based on Field-Circuit Coupled Iterations
abstract: The rapid development of rail transit has caused growing concern about metro stray current (MSC) intrusion in urban power grid (UPG). MSC intrusion inevitably causes risks such as transformer DC bias and grounding grid corrosion. Accurate evaluation of MSC intrusion current in UPG is crucial for addressing these challenges. Existing research indicates that MSC intrudes UPG through two distinct paths, respectively the metal sheath and the earth. Considering MSC in the metal path follows Kirchhoff’s law, while MSC in the earth path satisfies the electric field diffusion equation. Therefore, to accurately obtain MSC intrusion current distribution in UPG, we proposed an evaluation method for intrusion current in UPG caused by MSC based on field-circuit coupled iterations. Firstly, a metro-UPG dual network coupling model was established, including both the earth path and metal path. Based on resistive network and injection current of the model, the nodal voltage equation was formulated. Then, the earth potentials induced by MSC diffusion in the earth were obtained by the complex image method for each grounding branches. Next, the earth potentials were equivalent to current sources via Norton’s theorem, which in turn updates the injection current. Finally, MSC intrusion current was evaluated through iterating nodal voltage. The accuracy was verified with field results. Moreover, the critical path and influence factor of MSC intrusion current were analyzed. The proposed method supports the evaluation and suppression of MSC intrusion UPG.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Terminal DC System for Large-Scale Renewable Integration: Topology and Coordinated Control
abstract: As DC power projects transition toward phased construction and higher voltage levels, interconnecting existing systems to form a multi-voltage-level DC grid is a pragmatic choice that balances the wide-area integration of large-scale renewable energy with the maximization of legacy asset utilization. While DC/DC transformer (DCT) topologies provide viable technical paths, scaling them to ultra-high-voltage applications involves considerations such as full-scale hardware requirements and isolation transformer design. To facilitate more flexible phased expansion, this paper proposes a Hierarchical Multi-Terminal DC (HMTDC) system with Coordinated Primary and Secondary Control (CPSC). The topology employs Multi-Voltage-Level Interconnecting MMCs (MVLI-MMCs) rated for the inter-system voltage differential rather than full terminal voltage, enabling gigawatt-level power exchange through significantly reduced converter capacity. The CPSC combines distributed droop-based primary control for rapid disturbance rejection with secondary optimization that coordinates power margins and voltage quality across subsystems. Comprehensive time-domain simulations demonstrate that the proposed framework not only optimizes cross-level power flows but also ensures fault ride-through and rapid recovery under severe AC/DC contingencies, thereby providing a techno-economically viable pathway for evolving multi-voltage-level DC grids.

title: Self-Adaptive Physics-Informed Neural Network for Power Transformer Insulation Paper Degradation Based on Emsley's Model
abstract: This paper presents a predictive model based on a physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework to estimate the degree of polymerization (DP) in power transformer insulation paper. The PINN algorithm integrates two fundamental objectives: aligning predicted DP values with actual measurements through data-driven optimization and maintaining consistency with the mathematical model governing DP degradation, known as Emsley's model. Based on Emsley's model, the relationships between the model output (predicted DP value) and the three input variables (historical DP value, its corresponding time, and the prediction time) are formulated as a set of partial differential equations and incorporated into the proposed PINN framework. To enhance prediction accuracy, the training process is adaptive, dynamically adjusting the weighting factor of each objective within the loss function, resulting in a self-adaptive PINN (SAPINN). Additionally, this paper introduces a regional collocation point generation strategy in SAPINN to improve data mapping in periods during which industrial data is not available. The proposed SAPINN is trained and tested on industrial data collected from 83 transformers, each with an average of seven data points recorded annually over seven years. The obtained results indicate that the proposed SAPINN model achieved an average mean absolute error of 15.7, compared to 17.4 and 18.8 obtained using the standard PINN and a basic neural network, respectively. Furthermore, the accuracy of the proposed model is compared to that of multiple machine learning models, PINN with the basic Emsley's model, and the theoretical model, where the proposed SAPINN demonstrates greater reliability and robustness.

title: Redundant Submodule-based Valve-Side Single-Phase-to-Ground Fault Protection in MMC-MVDC Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper proposes a redundant submodule (SM)-based protection scheme for modular multilevel converter-based medium voltage dc (MMC-MVDC) distribution systems under valve-side single-phase-to-ground (SPG) faults. Both symmetrical monopolar and bipolar MMC station configurations are studied, considering half-bridge SMs (HBSMs), full-bridge SMs (FBSMs), and hybrid SMs for each converter station. Redundant SMs normally operate in bypass state and transition into a blocking state once a valve-side SPG fault is detected. In symmetrical monopolar MMCs, the use of unipolar redundant SMs can prevent upper and lower arm overvoltage following converter blocking. However, bipolar redundant SMs are required in the bipolar MMC to mitigate upper arm overvoltage in systems with HBSMs, FBSMs and hybrid SMs, lower arm overvoltage in systems with hybrid SMs, as well as to address the issue of non-zero crossings of grid-side currents in systems with HBSMs. Simulation results in PSCAD/EMTDC validate the effectiveness of the proposed redundant SM-based protection methods for MMC-MVDC distribution systems under valve-side SPG faults.

title: Impact of Thermal Cycling Variation on the Static Clamping Pressure in Transformer Test Rig
abstract: During the manufacturing of core-type power trans formers, the winding structure is clamped by horizontal clamping beams to withstand operational and through-fault current forces. The effects of evolving grid conditions, e.g., frequent switching cycles and increasingly dynamic load profiles, on the evolution of winding clamping pressure of transformers in operation are largely unknown. This paper investigates how different thermal cycles affect clamping pressure in a pressboard spacer–brass plate stack clamped within a test rig. To minimize the surface effects caused by the sieve structure of the pressboard spacers, the top and bottom cellulose plies have been machined off. In this paper, both oil-impregnated and non-impregnated dry pressboard spacers are studied. All spacers are first vacuum dried under a constant sizing pressure of 7 MPa, followed by oil-impregnation when applicable. Afterwards, the spacer-brass plate stack is assembled in the test rig with an initial clamping pressure of 4 MPa. To investigate the effect of different thermal cycling on the clamping pressure, three different heating rates are applied: low, medium, and high power. At least 15 heating cycles with a cooling phase in between are applied to each test case. It is observed that the loss of clamping pressure is most pronounced during the first heating cycle and gradually diminishes with subsequent cycles. When the initial effect is excluded, no clear relation between the heating rates and the loss of clamping pressure is observed. No significant influence of oil-impregnation on the evolution of clamping pressure is observed under the present test condition. The results highlight the importance of material treatment and initial clamping procedure during the transformer manufacturing process, as these factors significantly influence the clamping pressure and its long-term stability.

title: Electromagnetic Response Analysis of Gas-Insulated Transmission Lines Utilizing Cross-Dimensional Multi-Physics Coupling
abstract: The abnormal electromagnetic responses of Gas-Insulated Transmission Lines (GILs) pose a significant risk to equipment and grid safety; yet, the traditional full 3D electromagnetic analysis method is limited by computational efficiency and structural applicability. Thus, the paper introduces a cross-dimensional multi-physics coupling method to study the electromagnetic responses of single-phase and three-phase enclosed GILs under different operating conditions. First, a novel 2D nodal electromagnetic analysis model is developed, incorporating the field-circuit coupling strategy to clarify the electromagnetic responses. Second, a 3D model of GILs is constructed for structural field analysis. Through an electromagnetic-mechanical coupling strategy, cross-dimensional transmission of 2D nodal electromagnetic responses is achieved. Third, the use of a transient analysis method uncovers patterns of electromagnetic stress distribution. Finally, the findings are verified using Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and live examination experiments on GILs.

title: Protection of Series-Compensated Transmission Lines Connected to Inverter-Based Resources
abstract: The protection challenges and solutions for series-compensated transmission lines have been thoroughly investigated in the literature. In addition, many studies have highlighted the challenges posed by inverter-based resources (IBRs) to transmission line protection. However, the combined impacts of series compensation and IBRs on transmission line relays remain unexplored. This gap in research has significant practical implications, especially as inverter-based renewable energy sources are often located far from load centers, increasing the probability of series compensation in their vicinity. This paper investigates whether and how existing protection practices for series-compensated lines are influenced by the fault response of IBRs. The findings are relevant not only to the direct tie lines of IBRs but also to lines connected to parts of the grid where the generation is primarily inverter-based. The paper examines the distance and directional elements commonly used for transmission line protection. The analytical studies in this paper are supported by detailed PSCAD/EMTDC simulations of IBRs and series-compensated lines. The paper also presents comprehensive test results from commercial transmission line relays. The results demonstrate that the fault current characteristics of IBRs can invalidate key assumptions underlying existing protection solutions for series-compensated transmission lines, leading to potential misoperations of distance and directional elements. The paper identifies the root causes of these issues and discusses relay configuration strategies to achieve more reliable protection.

title: A Hybrid Multi-agent Fault Location Strategy in Active Distribution Network Using Synchrophasors
abstract: Locating faults and isolating the faulted sections of the network are integral to the smooth operation of any self healing distribution system. A novel multi-agent system based event location and isolation approach is proposed for a modern power distribution system using synchronized current and voltage from a limited number of PMUs. The developed multi-agent framework uses a decentralized hierarchical agent scheme and consists of heterogeneous agent types, with the PMUs defined as the main computational agents. The agents receive their local synchrophasor measurements and perform the algorithm by communicating with their neighboring agents to locate the faulted bus with minimal communication messages. The new fault location algorithm is a two-step process: first, the agents identify the faulted section using impedance comparison and isolate the faulted zone; second, the corresponding agents within the zone identify the faulted bus using voltage comparison and send the bus information to the control center. Studies are conducted by interconnecting the IEEE 34-bus network with distributed energy resources developed in PSCAD/EMTDC and a multi-agent system implemented on the JADE platform. Simulations of various test cases verify the efficacy of the proposed multi-agent scheme in accurately locating various faults occurring in the distribution network.

title: Equivalent Inertia Mechanism Modeling and Magnitude-Phase Characteristics Analysis of Grid-Supporting MMC-HVDC Systems
abstract: The grid-supporting MMC-HVDC systems emulate synchronous generator characteristics to enable efficient power transmission while providing frequency support. However, existing studies lack analytical insights into the equivalent inertia and time-varying supporting mechanism under different control strategies. To address this, an equivalent inertia analytical model for grid-supporting MMC-HVDC systems is firstly established from a frequency-domain perspective. The proposed models can accurately describe the equivalent inertia and the time-varying characteristics under different control modes, and their validity and correctness are verified through comparative simulation case studies. Based on the established model, the magnitude-phase supporting characteristics of grid-supporting MMC-HVDC are analyzed. The amplitude |HMMC(s)| is derived to evaluate the magnitude of inertia support capability provided by the MMC-HVDC, while the resonance frequency ωpeak is employed to analyze the phase-delay characteristics of the maximum inertia supporting power and the influence on frequency recovery. Besides, the supporting mechanism of different parameters on the equivalent inertia are analyzed, and the dominant characteristics of these parameters during different stages of frequency recovery is revealed. Simulation results validate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed model and conclusions.

title: Galloping Detection for AC Overhead Transmission Line Based on Induced Signals in Ground Wires
abstract: Conductor galloping threatens the safe operation of overhead transmission lines. This paper proposes an online monitoring method for galloping through the induced current or voltage in the ground wires, which is based on the periodic variation of mutual inductance between conductors and ground wires. The monitoring device of this method is convenient to install and maintain, and the monitoring effect is not influenced by bad weather such as fog and snow. In order to detect galloping information, a calculation model for the induced signals in the ground wires during galloping is firstly studied. Then the dynamic response of induced signals in the ground wires under different galloping conditions is analyzed. An inverse deduction method for galloping characteristics is then proposed based on the frequency features of the induced signals in the ground wires. A scaled test is conducted to verify the feasibility of the proposed method. The accuracy of deduced results is acceptable and the study offers new possibilities for overhead transmission line condition monitoring.

title: Field-Validated Accelerometer-Based Tension Estimation for Overhead Distribution Lines
abstract: This paper presents a proof-of-concept framework validated using field data that estimates the mechanical tension and corresponding sag of overhead distribution conductors using on-conductor accelerometers and a Random Forest (RF) model. One minute-resolution datasets were collected over a one-month period from three 30-m spans of a 22.9-kV-class distribution line test facility at the KEPCO Gochang Test Center under non-energized conditions. The direct sensor output channels (AccX, AccY, AccZ, Roll, and Yaw), together with temperature and wind variables, are used as inputs to the RF regressor. Across the three spans under the tested conditions, the RF model achieves the lowest normalized root mean square error and the highest coefficient of determination, with NRMSE in the range of 0.007–0.012 and R² values approaching unity for tension estimation. Sag is then computed from the estimated tension using a standard parabolic approximation consistent with IEEE Std 524. The resulting sag traces closely match those obtained from measured tension, with R² between 0.996 and 0.999 and mean sag errors in the few-millimeter range, well within the installation tolerances prescribed by IEEE Std 524. A rolling 5-fold cross-validation analysis shows small fold-to-fold dispersion within the available dataset, supporting the feasibility of the proposed framework as a proof-of-concept under the tested conditions. The proposed framework therefore demonstrates the feasibility of using accelerometer signals for tension and sag estimation and suggests potential applicability to clearance assessment and condition monitoring under similar operating conditions.

title: Finite-Time Convergent Adaptive Sliding Mode Control for Integration of VSCs Into Modernized Microgrids With Parametric and Dynamic Uncertainties
abstract: This research article presents an innovative approach to enhance the performance and robustness of voltage source converters within microgrid systems. Existing controls suffer from slow convergence and unsatisfactory transient performance when dealing with disturbances, especially in the presence of control delay. To discourse these limitations, the proposed sliding mode controller is augmented with a nonlinear disturbance observer to enhance the disturbance elimination capability, attenuates the effect of parameter uncertainties, superior voltage reference tracking and suppressing chattering in the control response. The observer is introduced to estimate sensor values, potentially eliminating the need for dedicated sensors. The proposed control strategy employs a switching Lyapunov function-based mathematical model, addressing dynamic response limitations and switching action incorporating nonlinearities in the proposed model. By incorporating Lyapunov-based stability analysis, the article overcomes limitations and conservatisms associated with traditional linearized techniques, enabling more accurate stability assessments. Online adaptation norms are integrated to estimate and reject external disturbances, aligning closed-loop responses with reference models. Extensive numerical simulations and hardware-in-the-loop experiments validate the improved performance, highlighting the elimination of chattering and enhanced robustness against step and stochastic disturbances.

title: Experimental Studies on Anti-Icing Properties of Anodized Conductors With Nanoporous Structures in Natural Environments
abstract: Anti-icing materials and conductors have been reported to exhibit icephobicity in laboratory conditions. However, practical engineering applications pose two significant challenges: i) the extended duration of natural icing (3-4 days) causes non-equivalence with short-term laboratory tests; ii) varied ice types make laboratory results hardly replicable to natural ice accretion. Here, anodized conductors with nanoporous structures were fabricated to achieve the desired anti-icing properties under the prolonged low-temperature and high-humidity natural icing conditions, even after one year of outdoor exposure. Notably, the anodized conductor demonstrated a significant reduction in ice weight during a full atmospheric icing period (150 hours), while also achieving effective ice-weight mitigation in the second-year tests, which involved 48 hours of glaze ice and 75 hours of hard-rime deposition. Moreover, the anodized conductor was implemented and validated on an operational 35 kV transmission line (several hundred meters). Meanwhile, field assessments on the electrical performance of the anodized ACSRs under the high-altitude natural environment validated improvements in corona inception voltages and heat dissipation at rated currents compared to bare ACSRs. Therefore, the proposed conductor represents a viable alternative to traditional overhead lines, promising effective icing mitigation and energy-efficient high-voltage transmission.

title: A Damage Prevention Device for Suspension Towers Subjected to Conductor Breakage
abstract: Suspension towers in high-voltage transmission lines are generally designed to sustain some damage during a sudden conductor breakage due to economic constraints. This study presents a novel device to be installed between an insulator and its supporting tower cross-arm to prevent such damage. The device is designed to act as a rigid link under normal operations and undergo large inelastic deformations during a conductor breakage, thereby dissipating energy and limiting the transferred force below the design lateral load capacity of the tower. Laboratory tests are conducted to experimentally characterize the device behavior and develop detailed continuum finite element models. A trilinear model of the device is then developed using basic principles of mechanics and dimensional analysis and the results of a comprehensive parametric FE simulation. The trilinear model is used to perform conductor breakage simulation of an existing 132 kV transmission line system. The results show that the proposed device can prevent damage to suspension towers and is well-suited to enhance the reliability of new and existing transmission line systems.

title: Research on the Influence of VFTO on Voltage Transformer in Electric Locomotives
abstract: Frequent insulation breakdown in voltage transformer (VT) is a critical issue that needs to be solved in the high-voltage electrical system of electric locomotives (HVES-EL). Existing research indicates that overvoltage is an important cause of insulation breakdown in VT. This paper firstly proposed an equivalent circuit model of the VT winding involving parasitic parameters. The parasitic parameters were determined by combining the finite element method and analytical calculations. Then we analyzed the switching overvoltage characteristics in the HVES-EL by establishing an equivalent simulation model. Finally, we studied the longitudinal voltage gradient distribution within the VT winding based on the equivalent circuit models of HVES-EL and VT. The results show that the switching overvoltage exhibits the characteristics of a high amplitude and steepness specific to very vast transient overvoltage (VFTO). The voltage distribution in the VT windings is extremely uneven under VFTO, the inter-layer voltage decays exponentially from the beginning to the end of the winding. The winding-to-ground voltage exhibits an oscillatory decay trend, with the maximum value occurring in the first layer. The results indicate that VFTO can easily lead to insulation breakdown between layers and turns near the VT's first layer of the winding, potentially inducing ferromagnetic resonance and causing thermal breakdown and damage to the VT. This study is of great significance for the insulation optimization design of the VT.

title: Inverter Based Resource With a Long Feeder: Modeling and Experimental Validation
abstract: This work presents a comprehensive analysis of Inverter-Based Resource (IBR) performance with long feeders. It is a configuration that has been increasingly common in several power system applications, ranging from renewable interconnections such as offshore wind farms to oil exploitation pumping systems. This work shows that simplified modeling approaches yield significant inaccuracies in predicting system behavior. Analysis reveals that an ideal IBR representation coupled with detailed feeder modeling fails to predict responses at the receiving end accurately. Similarly, detailed IBR modeling with simplified feeder representation also produces inadequate results. In the latter, the feeder is treated as a single-phase equivalent to frequency-dependent and distributed characteristics. Accurate system response prediction requires simultaneous consideration of the actual IBR voltage waveform and detailed feeder representation equivalent to those used in wideband transient testing. This integrated modeling approach captures the complex interactions between harmonic-rich IBR outputs and the distributed impedance characteristics of long feeders. The experimental results were carried out at an operational oil company facility housing the long-feeder. The feeder is a 12/20 kV, 2.5 km umbilical cable wound on a drum. Due to space restrictions in the facility, only a low-voltage IBR was used. It is connected to the feeder without an output filter to create a harmonic-rich environment. All the simulations were carried out using the Numerical Laplace Transform.

title: Influence of Loaded Power Cable Cyclic Transversal Bending on Trend Evolution of Dielectric Loss and Partial Discharges
abstract: Zero-emission goals necessitate future global energy strategies to rely on renewable energy sources. As a result, significant investments are being directed toward large-scale offshore wind farms around the world. This has led to substantial advancements and growing demand for submarine cables for linking these offshore farms to the power grids (especially, a new class that refers to floating cables that are exposed to cyclic or fluctuating mechanical stresses). In this article, investigations on the influence of a loaded power cable's transversal bending on its performance indicators during cyclic transversal bending are presented. During the tests, phase-resolved partial discharge (PD), dielectric-loss, and cable temperature measurements were simultaneously performed. The original concept was a real-time synchronous correlation of the above markers recorded up to the cable's electrical breakdown during consecutive bending cycles. The loaded cable temperature evolution was analyzed in correlation with the performance indicators and the number of bending cycles. The article presents an original methodology for measuring and assessing trends, along with a quantitative framework for analyzing the degradation of dynamic cables. The individual stages of cable degradation, such as the cracking of the wires in both the cable core and the outer screen as well as insulation deterioration, were identified and correlated with the dielectric loss waveforms and PD patterns. The methodology and results may contribute to the testing and diagnostics of dynamic power cables that are exposed to frequent mechanical movements during normal operations, such as in industry, mining, and (particularly) subsea applications. This is especially relevant for future submarine dynamic cables, which will demand enhanced mechanical and electrical durability.

title: Novel Bushing With Adaptively Field Grading Structure: Experiment and Validation
abstract: In the previous part, simulation works were conducted to analyze the field grading effect of nonlinear materials in the application of bushing, and the aim of this paper is to present the experimental investigations. The adaptive field grading (AFG) bushing samples are prepared by a novel method based on wet winding technology, and the assembly quality is verified by scanning electron microscope, thermal gravimetric analyzer, and conductivity test of slice samples with multi-layered structure. The initial partial discharge voltage and phase-resolved partial discharge pattern characteristics of the AFG bushing samples are obtained. Taking S0 without a field grading layer as the control group, it exhibited noticeable internal partial discharge at 36 kV. At the same time, S2 and S3 samples with nonlinear materials had higher initial partial discharge voltages, which are 66.67% and 38.89% higher than those of the former samples, respectively. The insulation strengths under the lightning impulse voltage of the AFG bushing samples are also tested. The S0 sample was broken down under severe high-voltage impulses, while the S2 sample remained well-insulated after 15 positive and negative lightning impulses. It is hoped that this work will provide an innovative technical roadmap for bushing design and manufacturing.

title: Performance Enhancement of Grid-Connected Photovoltaic Systems: Addressing Nonlinear Load Challenges
abstract: Photovoltaic (PV)-based consumer-end power generation supports sustainable development and is typically grid-connected to minimize dependence on bulky energy storage systems. However, modern power electronics-based local loads significantly degrade system performance, especially under weak grid conditions. Conventional control methods struggle to maintain grid current quality during disturbances on the grid, PV, or load side, and often lack the required dynamic responsiveness. This paper proposes a fast and robust grid integration control strategy for injecting PV array power into the grid while enhancing grid current quality in the presence of both load-side and grid-side disturbances. The proposed method utilizes a dual second-order generalized integrator (SOGI) to synthesize balanced, steady, and sinusoidal three-phase reference grid currents-even under distorted grid conditions-while inherently rejecting measured voltage's harmonics, imbalance and DC offsets. This eliminates the need for additional integrals or complex feedback loops, thereby overcoming the limitations of conventional SOGI-based methods. Furthermore, a least mean square (LMS)-based algorithm is employed to extract the active power component of the load current, enabling auxiliary active power support via a PI controller and enhancing the system's dynamic response to load variations. The proposed strategy is implemented in a weak-grid-connected PV system supplying nonlinear battery charging loads without dedicated harmonic compensation hardware, and its superior performance is validated through experimental results on a laboratory prototype.

title: Optimal Polygon-Closure Mechanism: A Cost-Minimized Solution for Filtering Multiple Harmonic Sources in Energy Routers
abstract: Energy routers (ERs) are an efficient technology for deploying renewable microgrids, especially in isolated regions. Secondary harmonic currents (SHCs) from unbalanced inverters cause low-frequency oscillations in the operating points of sources and loads, reducing their performance and lifespan. Existing filtering solutions require manufacturers to deploy large-capacity active power filters (APFs) in multiple SHC scenarios, incurring unacceptably high expenses. This paper introduces an optimal polygon-closure mechanism that intrinsically links SHC filtering to polygon shape optimization. Within this framework, optimal filtering—minimizing the SHC absorption by APF while preserving AC-side power quality and completely filtering SHCs—corresponds to forming a closed polygon with the minimal perimeter. First, a polygon shaping strategy is proposed to minimize the polygon perimeter by adjusting SHC phases. This effectively reduces the SHC required to be absorbed by APF to zero or below the largest single SHC, enabling the elimination of multiple SHCs using a low-capacity filter. Second, a polygon closure strategy is designed to ensure polygon closure by using APFs to absorb the SHC. This method enables accurate and complete SHC filtering and provides the essential functions of harmonic sharing, plug-and-play operation, and applicability to both step-up and step-down APFs. The solution enables the APF capacity to be determined by the maximum SHC among all individual branches rather than the aggregate of the maximum SHCs from all branches, substantially cutting APF installation costs. Simulation results in RT-LAB confirm that the proposed method significantly reduces the APF filtering burden, achieves complete SHC elimination, does not impair transient control, and reduces APF capacity by 54.55% in a real-world project involving three harmonic sources.

title: Final Jump Impulses in Negative Stepped Leader Cloud to Ground Lightning
abstract: The paper constitutes a model of the final jump that occurs during the encounter between a negative downward stepped leader and an upward connecting leader in cloud to ground lightning. The gap is first covered by negative and positive streamers, followed by leader bridging. Voltage collapse yields substantial impulse current determined by both the gap and stepped leader characteristics. A model is formulated for the leader bridging and subsequent current impulse flow, during which the negative downward leader is simulated as a lossy transmission line. Within the range of variables investigated the following findings are reported. With neutral charge point in the cloud at a height of 4500 m, ambient ground field of 8 kV/m, a 10 m ground mast and prospective return stroke current in the range of 10-100 kA, the model resulted in final jump gaps in the range of 7-27 m. The average leader bridging speed is found to vary in the range of 5-16 m/μs. The final jump impulse current is evaluated in the 2-12 kA range corresponding to 10-20% of the subsequent prospective return stroke current. The final jump impulse current is therefore substantially larger than the preceding corona bursts. The input surge impedance of the downward leader at the instant of final jump varies in the range 1.6 kohm to 2.8 kohm. Results with a height of charge cloud point origin Hcs of 2500 m have been added and showed very significant increase in the final jump gap length and impulse current amplitude but a moderate reduction in the leader input surge impedance. The discharge phase of the final jump is therefore established as a distinct prerequisite for the formation of the return stroke. In principle the final jump impulse current can be measured on instrumented towers, discarding prior upward leader current and corona pulses from adjacent branches. It can also be estimated from remote electric field measurement, with due consideration to the specific speed of the resulting signal propagating along the stepped leader. In this paper whenever possible comparison of the model results with field measurement is made and found satisfactory.

title: Investigation of the External Thermal Resistance of Cables in Backfills and Duct Banks
abstract: The Neher/McGrath paper and IEC Standard 60287-2-1 provide formulas for calculating the external thermal resistance of cables installed in backfills or duct banks. In this context, the backfill or duct bank is represented as a circular isothermal surface, assuming that the thermal resistances of both are equivalent. The 2023 edition of IEC Standard 60287-2-1 introduces a table of geometric factors to calculate the radius of the equivalent circle. In contrast, earlier editions relied on an analytical formula that assumed the backfill's width-to-height ratio was between 1/3 and 3. This paper investigates modeling problems arising from the application of the new IEC standard 60287-2-1 to cables installed in duct banks and backfills. The findings indicate that assumptions in the IEC standard for modeling the external thermal resistance of cables may lead to significant errors. As a result, the paper proposes a new approach that addresses weaknesses in the standard approach. The new approach is verified through a finite-element analysis. Several numerical examples illustrate the differences between the proposed approach and the results based on the standard analysis.

title: Waveform Distortions During Power Frequency Testing of Metal Oxide Varistors: Their Origin and Effect on Average Power Dissipation
abstract: While it is well known that a Metal Oxide Varistor (MOV) heavily distorts the voltage wave of a high-current lightning impulse, less has been said about waveform distortions observed during power frequency testing. This paper shows that significant distortions are likely produced by practical generators during power frequency testing of MOVs, with the effect that average power dissipation of MOVs and surge arresters is severely impacted by generator setup. Four distribution transformer configurations with different output impedances were used to apply 60 Hz voltage waves to a conducting, 5 kV-rated MOV at six peak current levels. Distortion was found to be a function of generator impedance and current magnitude. In one typical experiment, even a slight distortion (Vrms / (Vpeak / √2) = 1.014) led to ∼33% decrease in average power dissipation compared to that of a distortion-free wave of the same rms voltage. Without consideration of these effects, seemingly minor differences in procedure can cause parts to erroneously pass or fail tests prescribed in IEEE C62.11 (2020) or IEC 60099-4 ed. 3.0, leading to arresters not meeting manufacturers’ 60 Hz TOV claims. A method is also outlined to correct for waveform distortion, enabling calculation of distortion-free average power dissipation.

title: Gas-Blasting Effects on Contact Erosion in Self-Blast-Type High-Voltage Circuit Breakers: Experimental Study and Mechanistic Insights
abstract: During the current interruption process in high-voltage circuit breakers, gas-blasting effects interact with arc-electrode phenomena and these affect each other. This paper presents an experimental study on Cu-W arcing contacts in a self-blast-type gas circuit breaker, at current peak values of 5 kA, 20 kA and 35 kA representing low, medium, and high current conditions. Mass loss measurements are complemented by surface morphology analysis to elucidate erosion mechanisms. The results show that erosion behavior is governed by the combined influence of electrode surface temperature and gas flow. When the contact temperature remains below the tungsten melting point, the tungsten skeleton offers strong resistance to erosion. Once a molten pool forms, however, gas-blasting significantly accelerates material removal, leading to increased mass loss. These findings provide mechanistic insight into erosion processes under gas-blasting conditions and establish a baseline reference in SF6 for future comparative studies in alternative gases such as CO2-based mixtures.

title: Downscaling Method for Ground Flash Density in Transmission Line Corridors Considering Terrain Effects
abstract: Ground Flash Density (GFD) serves as a critical parameter for evaluating the lightning strike risk of transmission lines.  It is typically derived from the statistical analysis of data monitored by Lightning Location Systems. However, constrained by the limited sample size of ground flashes and the detection accuracy of Lightning Location Systems, the spatial resolution of GFD is relatively low. To enhance the spatial resolution of GFD along transmission line corridors, this paper proposes a downscaling method of GFD based on the Monte Carlo method considering micro-terrain conditions. For a given original grid area, considering the influence of terrain on lightning, the lightning strike point is determined by the lightning leader fractal model, thereby generating a simulated dataset of ground flash samples dataset. The original grid is further divided into multiple subunits, and the GFD of subunit is calculated by combining the grid average ground flash density statistics, ultimately yielding the high spatial resolution ground flash density. The proposed method is used to calculate GFD in the actual grid area and the effectiveness of the method is verified.

title: Research on metal particle morphology identification in GIS based on optical sensing and multi-task learning
abstract: Metal particle contamination is a primary factor triggering surface discharge in gas insulated switchgear (GIS). Existing studies predominantly focus on identifying insulation defect types while lack refined diagnosis of particle morphological characteristics. To address this, a synchronous measurement system of optical and electrical signals based on silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) is first constructed, and the characteristics of surface discharge optical pulses of linear, flaky and elliptical particles under various sizes and different position conditions are systematically studied in a 126 kV real GIS. The temporal characteristics and phase-resolved distribution patterns of optical pulses under different particle morphologies are elucidated. Building upon these findings, a novel multi-task learning framework integrating lightweight convolution and a customized gating mechanism is proposed. By deeply exploring the mapping relationship between phase-resolved discharge patterns and particle morphology, this framework achieves simultaneous identification of particle shape and size. Compared with conventional single-task learning models, the proposed framework achieves better shape and size identification accuracy (93.70% and 96.00%) with lower computational cost, which is 6.62% and 2.92% higher than the single-task learning model, respectively. The framework exhibits superior comprehensive performance over other multi-task learning models and operates efficiently on edge computing devices (average runtime: 14.37 ms), offering a promising technical solution for refined condition assessment and intelligent monitoring of GIS.

title: Improved Lumped-Parameter Thermal Network Modeling for Rapid Temperature Rise Evaluation of Horizontal Single-Phase Gas-Insulated Transmission Lines Considering Distributed Thermal Convection
abstract: Gas-insulated transmission lines (GIL) are valued as an alternative to overhead lines and cables in specific applications due to their high reliability, minimal electromagnetic interference, and substantial transmission capacity. Operational temperature rise directly affects system reliability, safety, and longevity. Meanwhile, rising power demands require improved accuracy and efficiency in GIL temperature rise evaluation. To balance computational precision and complexity in GIL thermal analysis, an improved lumped-parameter thermal network (LPTN) modeling strategy that considers the distributed thermal convection of insulating gas under the combined influence of gravity and buoyancy forces is proposed. The method simplifies gas convection effects under gravity and buoyancy influences into equivalent thermal conduction terms by integrating convection parameters, skin effect factors, and other key variables. The structural framework of the model is constructed through the analysis of the heat transfer mechanism and thermal pathways. Control equations are then derived via time-domain analysis based on fundamental physical principles. Validation against prototype experimental data shows a maximum temperature rise error of the LPTN model below 8.29%, which is comparable to the accuracy of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation. Furthermore, compared to CFD, the model reduces computational time by approximately 2000-fold. These results demonstrate that it provides a highly accurate and efficient solution for thermal characteristics analysis of GIL.

title: Multiphysical Field Simulation and Experimental Verification of Initial Stage of Tree-Contact Arc Grounding Fault in Distribution Networks
abstract: Due to tree growth and wind-induced disturbances, tree-contact arc grounding faults (TAGFs) occur frequently in distribution networks. In the initial stage of the fault, the fault signal is weak and can frequently be undetected by protective devices. Therefore, a multiphysics simulation model coupling arc plasma behavior with distribution system response is developed based on magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) theory. The influences of tree species, moisture content, and branch swing velocity on arc temperature, morphology, and fault current amplitude are analyzed. A time-domain energy balance analysis is conducted to reveal the mechanisms underlying current zero-crossing behavior. Experimental results validate the model’s ability to accurately reproduce key TAGF features, including high fault impedance, arc temperature fluctuations, and neutral-point voltage oscillations. The findings provide a physically interpretable foundation for early detection and suppression of TAGFs in ungrounded distribution systems.

title: An Analytic Method for Frequency Nadir Estimation in Fast Frequency Response Resource (FFRR) Dominant Power Systems
abstract: This paper proposes an analytic method for estimating frequency nadir in power systems dominated by fast frequency response resources (FFRRs). The proposed method approximates the frequency response of FFRRs, which could be either complex or whose internal logic is not disclosed generally. This is because commercial-level models are typically provided as black box systems in large power system analysis. With the approximated transfer function, the frequency response following a major disturbance is represented by a simple equation that resembles the general solution for a second-order system's impulse response. The proposed method is validated through case studies of Jeju Island's power system in South Korea, employing user-defined models (UDMs) for high-voltage direct current (HVDC) systems. Results demonstrate that the proposed method predicts frequency nadir with high accuracy, which is almost identical with those of PSS/E.

title: A Unified Reliability Modeling Framework for MMC Considering Flexible Submodule Configuration and Preventive Maintenance
abstract: Conventional analytical models for engineering-scale modular multilevel converters (MMCs) face significant challenges in reliability assessment, particularly in incorporating preventive maintenance (PM) and redundancy. This paper proposes a simulation-based reliability modeling approach using the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method, which tracks the system level operational state evolution while considering PM. The approach enables the determination of reliability indices for engineering-scale systems and identifies the optimal fixed PM intervals and redundancy submodule (SM) configurations. Furthermore, it enables flexible adjustment of both the number and type of SMs within a unified framework for reliability assessment. Based on extensive simulation and validation, the method demonstrates its effectiveness in supporting reliability analysis and system design, offering a general framework for practical applications.

title: Fault Analysis and Pilot Protection Scheme for Various Single-Phase Line Breaks in Resonant Grounding Systems
abstract: Due to small fault currents and different fault characteristics under various grounding types on both sides of the fault point, the existing methods are facing challenges in the analysis and protection principle for single-phase break faults (SPBFs) in resonant grounding systems (RGSs), including inaccurate fault identification, low sensitivity, and insufficient reliability under high-impedance grounding and intermittent arc faults. In this paper, fault characteristics of zero-sequence voltages upstream and downstream of the break point with different grounding modes are analyzed. The SPBFs with grounding at single-side and without grounding only exhibit the amplitude or phase characteristic, while SPBFs with grounding at both sides incorporate the two features. On this basis, a pilot protection scheme is developed for various SPBFs in RGSs, where internal and external SPBFs are determined by combining the features of the amplitude and phase of dual-terminal zero-sequence voltages. The effectiveness of the proposed methodology is validated through a closed-loop hardware test by applying a real-time digital simulator (RTDS) and the developed protective devices. Experimental results prove that the protection scheme performs well under different fault types, fault locations, fault resistances, and the presence of inverter-interfaced distributed generators.

title: Substation Planning Method Based on a Novel Combinational Optimization Method Considering Incentive-Based Demand Response
abstract: Demand response (DR) is a significant resource for peak shaving of substations. However, substation capacity is strongly coupled with DR, which remains to be investigated. In this paper, a novel substation planning method considering incentive-based demand response is proposed. A nested substation planning framework based on combinational optimization is established, and the interdependence between substation capacity, service area and DR is incorporated. A systematic iterative solution algorithm is proposed, in which service area of substations are determined by hierarchical weighted Voronoi diagram method. Numerical experiments are carried out on a real rural region. Compared with mathematical optimization method and traditional weighted Voronoi diagram method, the solution quality and efficiency of the proposed method are improved.

title: Single Ended Fault Location of MMC-HVDC Lines Incorporating Traveling Wave and Model Information
abstract: This paper presents a single ended fault location (FL) scheme for MMC-HVDC transmission lines. The proposed method works with a relatively low sampling rate of 20 kHz, which corresponds to insufficient time resolution and generates large systematic error if applying traveling wave (TW) based FL methods. The proposed FL method can be seen as a fusion of TW based methods and model based methods. To mitigate the impact of fault resistance (FR) on FL accuracy, the fault current contribution from the remote end is accurately compensated based on the MMC equivalent source model. Specifically, since the MMC equivalent source model at the remote end is activated exactly when the TW arrives, the insufficient time resolution with the relatively low sampling rate will cause FL error. To tackle this challenge, the TW arrival time can be further fine-tuned by incorporating model information, enabling accurate FL even during high resistance faults. Simulation results verify that the proposed approach presents small fault location errors during both low resistance faults (LRFs) and high resistance faults (HRFs), and demonstrates robustness towards measurement noises and parameter errors.

title: Quantitative Metrics for Evaluating Grid Strength Across Power System Stability Domains: A Review
abstract: The increasing integration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) is reducing grid strength, making accurate assessment essential for reliable and stable power system operation. Quantitative metrics offer systematic and practical tools for evaluating grid strength, supporting both planning and operational decisions. This paper provides a comprehensive review of quantitative metrics for grid strength assessment across static, small-signal, and transient stability domains. Metrics are categorized and discussed in terms of their definitions, derivation methods, advantages, and limitations, with particular attention to the effects of IBR interactions, network topology, and control strategies. Relevant stability criteria, practical applicability, and recommended threshold values are also summarized. This review aims to support system planners and operators in selecting and applying appropriate grid strength metrics in power systems with high IBR penetration.

title: Defect Diagnosis Criterion for the Cross-Bonding Metallic Sheath Grounding System of 110 kV Power Cables
abstract: Cable sheath grounding systems account for a high proportion of high-voltage power cable system defects. Currently, defect diagnosis criteria for power cable metallic sheaths are imprecise, which makes it difficult to identify defects in time and avoid losses. This paper proposes a diagnostic criterion to identify power cable metallic sheath defects through the sheath current in a cross-bonding sheath grounding system. A calculation method that integrates the theories of multiconductor transmission lines, finite element electromagnetic field calculations and two-port circuit networks is established. This method is accurate, flexible and quick; consequently, the probability distributions of the sheath currents with every defect and three random factors are obtained. Using the probability density function of the characteristic variables for normal and defect sheath grounding systems, the diagnosis criterion of the defect type is formulated on the basis of the minimum error rate criterion.

title: Calculation and Verification of Wind-induced Deflection Risk for Transmission Lines Based on High-precision Point Cloud Data
abstract: Wind-induced deflection has become a leading cause of faults in transmission lines under extreme weather conditions. This paper proposes a computational method for accurately assessing wind-induced deflection risk by leveraging high-precision point cloud data. First, the residual clustering algorithm was applied to extract the point clouds of individual power lines from the high-precision dataset, and a corresponding catenary equation was formulated. Next, tower contours, type identification, and structural parameters were extracted through an integrated approach combining the Alpha Shapes algorithm with the PointNet++ deep learning network. Subsequently, a wind-induced deflection calculation and evaluation model based on the finite element method was rapidly constructed, and its accuracy was validated through a dedicated wind-induced deflection test platform. Moreover, a Python-ANSYS co-simulation platform was developed to enable parametric modeling and automated solving of finite element models, substantially enhancing computational efficiency. Finally, by analyzing a wind-induced deflection fault case of a 500 kV transmission line, the effectiveness of the proposed point cloud-based wind-induced deflection assessment methodology was confirmed.

title: Fault Localization in Complex Power Grids: Addressing EMTR Limitations Through Strategic Sensor Placement
abstract: The Electromagnetic Time Reversal (EMTR) method has been receiving a lot of attention in the last years as an effective method to localize faults in electrical grids by analyzing transient signals induced by the fault. In this paper we first underline some of the limitations of EMTR when applied in real networks. Then, we propose a new metric based on spectrum similarity between the recorded signal and the fault-to-sensor frequency response of the network. Unlike similar approaches in the literature, this metric requires no information regarding the fault instant. Afterwards, we argue the need of multiple sensors to address the limitations of fault observability in complex network topologies. A novel algorithm for optimal sensor placement is introduced, which uses observability indices to determine the most effective sensor locations. This ensures maximum fault detection coverage, even in networks characterized by significant characteristic impedance variations between overhead lines and underground cables. Extensive simulations on two real medium-voltage distribution networks consisting of 32 and 161 buses respectively, are performed to illustrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach.

title: Air-Core Dry-Type Shunt Reactor: Modeling and Inter-Turn Fault Detection
abstract: This study presents an integrated approach for detecting inter-turn faults in air-core dry-type shunt reactors. It combines finite-element modeling with a data-driven protection scheme that utilizes the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) algorithm. The method was applied to a 230 kV air-core reactor installed at the Penedo bus of the Nossa Senhora do Socorro-Penedo transmission line in Brazil. Finite-element analysis was used to determine the reactor's self and mutual inductances under various inter-turn fault conditions. These analyses served as the foundation for time-domain transient simulations. Fault signatures were generated using MATLAB, while external events, such as transmission line faults, busbar faults, reclosing operations, nearby equipment energization, line oscillations, and voltage unbalances, were simulated in ATP to enhance the model's security. The XGBoost-based protection scheme was trained and tested with both internal and external cases, including scenarios with noise, to evaluate its robustness. Results demonstrated high accuracy, dependability, and security, with most faults detected within two cycles. This proposed method effectively identifies inter-turn faults, even in situations where conventional protection schemes exhibit limited sensitivity.

title: An Energy Differential Protection Scheme for Three-Stage SST AC-Side Outgoing Lines with Submodule Capacitor Energy Compensation
abstract: Protection of AC-side outgoing lines in three-stage solid-state transformers (SSTs) is challenging because control driven port currents undermine conventional current differential criteria, while overcurrent schemes are sensitive to transition resistance. This paper focuses on the phase-to-phase and three phase short-circuit faults, which are typically severe and require fast, reliable discrimination. Energy-differential protection offers a promising alternative; however, its direct application to SSTs is affected by substantial, control-dependent internal energy variations—mainly associated with submodule capacitors—which may delay internal-fault operation or trigger maloperation under external faults. This paper proposes an energy-differential protection scheme for three-stage SST AC-side outgoing lines with submodule-capacitor energy compensation. The proposed method suppresses the influence of internal energy dynamics without increasing setting margins or requiring additional measurement points. Its effectiveness is verified via MATLAB/Simulink simulations and RT-LAB real-time tests, demonstrating improved tolerance to transition resistance and enhanced noise immunity compared with existing methods.

title: A Novel Ice-Melting Method for Overhead Ground Wires of Transmission Lines Based on Scott Transformer
abstract: The mechanical strength of the overhead ground wire is lower than that of the transmission conductor, making it a vulnerable component in the face of transmission line icing disasters. Therefore, the research of ice-melting methods for overhead ground wires is of great importance for maintaining the safe and stable operation of transmission lines and power systems. Based on the single-loop and double-loop characteristics of overhead ground wire ice-melting circuits, we propose an ice-melting method for overhead ground wires based on the Scott transformer. Particularly targeting the single-loop ice-melting scenarios, which are more common and technically challenging in engineering practice, impedance matching is employed to establish the equivalent symmetrical load, which enables the effective ice-melting of the single-loop overhead ground wire ice-melting circuit. Furthermore, taking into account the impedance range of overhead ground wires and the required ice-melting current, parameter design principles for key equipment, including the Scott transformer, adjustable capacitors, and impedance matching components, are presented. Finally, the equipment parameters for different voltage levels are determined through case analysis, and the proposed method is validated by simulations on PSCAD/EMTDC platform. The results show that the proposed method can effectively satisfy the ice-melting requirements of overhead ground wires without introducing unbalanced current into the power grid, thereby providing reliable technical support for overhead ground wire ice-melting in various icing regions.

title: Degradation, Lifetime, and Failure Modes of Metal Oxide Varistors in Low-Voltage DC Circuit Breaker Applications
abstract: The metal oxide varistor (MOV) has been a critical enabling component for emerging applications in low-voltage dc circuit breakers (LVDCCBs). Although its properties align well with this application, its long-term performance, including degradation, failure modes, and service lifetime, remains poorly understood. Based on an accelerated degradation test (ADT) platform, this work collects extensive data to track degradation patterns and identify failure modes using statistical methods. A power-function-based model is proposed to identify the driving forces behind degradation, and a complete lifetime map of LVDCCB MOVs is achieved. The model predicts the lifetime of LVDCCB MOVs with a confidence level of 79.18%. The model and statistical analysis indicate that charge is the driving force for the defined failure mode, which needs to be addressed in the LVDCCB design while energy drives the catastrophic failure mode, which needs to be avoided in the LVDCCB design.
